written_by_Sean_Cavanaugh.Excerpt1: Your fiancé is a bad-ass salcedense who doesn't believe in letting shit slide. She catches you cheating (Well, more like she busts you out. Let’s be honest: You were sloppy.) After you left her your phone, she discovered that this papi chulo of hers is full of shit—you've cheated not with one, not two, but fifty pendejas!! She doesn’t scream, which would have been better; she sits silent through the whole awful exchange. She couldn't even get through all the archived emails, but she tracked the first one back six years.Bad move on your part, because she told you from the beginning that if you ever cheated on her she would chop your little pito off. But you cheated anyway. So she probably should leave you out in the cold. But she holds you down for a few months because the two of you, you know, are survivors. You saw her through her father’s death, the bar exam and she saw you through las plagas. You know the plagas: no job, poisoned liver, too long without a novel, too much time in the night clinic at Holy Name. But fukú doesn’t always strike like thunder. Sometimes it works patiently, drowning a nigger by degrees, like with the Chinese water torture. You travel to the D.R., to Mexico, to New Zealand. On a beach in the latter (the same one from the end of Jane Campion's The Piano that she always wanted to see), she walks out onto the sand and wraps her arms around herself in a way that seems utterly familiar to you, and when you try to hold her she says 'Please don't.' You drive back to the motel instead, and a couple of honeymooners—giddy with how much they are in love—pull up next to you. Their constant smiling makes you feel like screaming. That night, you hear her crying in the bathroom.
written_by_Sean_Cavanaugh.Excerpt2: You come home. It’s hot--dead hot, like a puta in church. She’s home, and rat-fucking pissed, but that’s what you liked about her, isn’t it? Bad-ass salcedense, short hair, ass is the stuff of rumors. Throw a brick at a homeboy for looking at her funny. And this salcedense had to throw a couple bricks in her day. But she found out, and it’s bad. Fifty women bad, and for six years. Plus you knew. Of course you fucking knew. She told you, you chancla-headed fuck, you slip once and she’s out. Well, cue the platano peel, because homie, you slipped. Fifty fucking girls. Once a year that’s half a siglo. She’s pissed, but it’s weird. Actually, you find out it’s chill. At least for a few months. Steady as it goes. Knew her too long, it turns out, through the job search, the bar, her father’s entierro. Can’t let go of a good thing. Even when she knows it’s bad. You kick off like that’ll help and hit the DR, CDM, fucking New Zealand. In NZ, fifty miles from Baggins Way, she says she dreamed this beach. Says it was in The Piano. She walks by herself and you watch her. Well, you try not to. You walk up and say baby, baby, grab her ass, make a kiss like you mean it. But she’s cooked. She’s fried. She wants nothing to do with your black ass. What I’m sayin is negro, you’ve fucked up bad. On the way to the hotel, you see this couple, right? H-O-N-E-Y-M-O-O-N. Eyes like the ocean, can’t keep off each other. Like he’d throw his ass into Mordor before he hurt his bae. Like this is what it’s supposed to be. I don’t gotta tell you how that makes you feel. When you get back, she starts crying. Making fists, the whole thing. She says you’re not no fucking man. Her daddy warned her about you. But he’s fuckin dead.

The first response is far superior to the second due to its consistent voice that portrays emotion well, rather than the second response that leans very heavily on strange slang and swearing to try to deliver the same message. The second is very performative, and feels more chaotic than the first, which maintains its impact throughout. This feels more about what excerpt 2 did incorrectly, rather than what excerpt 1 did correctly, for example:

"Throw a brick at a homeboy for looking at her funny."

written_by_Caroline_Porter.Excerpt1: You’ve been cheating on your fiance, a bad-ass salcedense from the DR who by all accounts doesn’t deserve it. Why? Because you’re some sort of idiot hijo de cuero, but you knew that about yourself long before she found the emails. Fifty women jammed into six years–it’s almost impressive, when you think about it. Or maybe it’s impressive when you don’t think about it too much. Your chiquita certainly doesn’t think it is–One rule, she spits at you through the expletives, one fucking rule. If you cheated on her, she was outta there. Except she wasn’t outta there–she lingers for a few months, like you are a cough she can’t quite shake. You’ve been through so much together–the death of her father, all your job problems, her rivalry and eventual defeat of the bar exam. You have history, and history doesn’t just go away. Someone has to erase it out of the books, and you sure as hell aren’t going to be the one to do it. And so you jet around the world to prove your love–the Dominican Republic, Mexico, all the way to fucking New Zealand where, on the beach from the movie The Piano, a place she’s always dreamed of going, she walks alone and barefoot on the sand in front of you, her sandals dangling from her fingers. You try to touch those fingers, her waist, her shoulder, but each time she pushes you away with a hiss, the wind lashing her long dark hair against her face, turning her into someone you don’t recognize. To make matters worse, you come across a couple while out for a ride together later that day, so all over each other and stupidly in love that it makes you question why you are here, why she is here, why you were both even born. She watches their love with a thin-lipped, dead-eyed expression. It is only later, in the privacy of your hotel room, that she cries.

written_by_Connor.Excerpt1: Craving and its indulgence are really one and the same thing. There might be no fruits, and still, if one wished for them, yearned for them, one would taste them all. The very sight of a berry in the wild is an admonishment not to pick it, for when it is stored in the vision and played upon by desire, the taste it bears is gifted to it as much by memory as by its savor. The flavor grows until it is too exquisite for the tongue, unencumbered by flesh. So it is when one wishes for a friend, or a woman, or a child. For Sylvie disappeared and made no sound, and I fancied when I had closed my eyes and rocked awhile that she was not gone. It was easier than I could have imagined to pretend I was not alone, to insist that she merely watched me from the woods. The wind was dying, the sun was sinking, the side of the house was cooling, the evening moths were glancing and settling, and her absence was a thing so full of longing it became a presence of its own. If I could row the lake at dawn and gather all the proud blossoms from the woods for one year, I would throw some across the graves of unsanctified and dreamless children and some into the holes of fox dens. And with the rest I would sculpt from snow a statue of a woman. I would stand her in the clearing in the woods, and she would be adorned with rare flowers with leaves like hands, with hardstem thistles, and the birds would rest in her. Lot's wife would have none of this: flowers in profusion and children. Her breast caved into a hollow of regret. Not this one, not my mother. written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: There are times when to long for something is almost as satisfying as to finally receive it, or when the essence of that which is desired is evoked so clearly that to receive it is no longer necessary. As when one yearns to pluck a berry from the vine and savor its ripeness, so that the sweetness seems to precede the taste of the juice itself. Yet in some way, I felt I could sense her closeness and thought she might be watching me from the woods, so I showed no change in my expression and pretended to be ignorant of my solitude. Around me, the sun cast long shadows through the partings of the tree branches, from which the browned leaves had already begun to fall into the clearing. A thin layer of frost was formed on the mud around where I sat. I imagined forming out of this cold clay earth a statue of a woman whom I would adorn with rare flowers. She would be a calm presence standing among the trees, not the cold, hard pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was transformed as punishment for her desire, for turning back with regret to look at all she had lost. A figure free of yearning, around whom the wild children of the forest would gather to marvel at her beauty and warmth. They would take solace in the vivacious beauty of such a figure and cling to her almost as a mother, even as her frozen hands could not caress them as one would their own children. Again I looked for Sylvie and thought of how I was, in searching for someone who had left me, not unlike the poor woman who had been turned to salt. Unlike the taste of those imagined berries, I was not sure if my longing for connection could ever be quite enough to evoke the presence of the thing itself.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: I’ve realized that craving and fulfillment are not connected in the way I once thought. A craving is so intense and visceral that it cannot be truly satiated by consuming the thing you want. For example, berries are always sweeter before I eat them. I wonder if that’s how Eve felt in the garden after she tasted the forbidden fruit—disappointed, hungry, running her tongue over her teeth in search of satisfaction. I’ve been thinking about Sylvie, and how she disappeared silently into the forest and left me alone. I suspected she might be hiding somewhere, watching from a perch atop a spruce tree or huddled inside a hollow log. She liked to tease me. I didn’t want to give her the satisfaction of calling out for her, making her think I was afraid of being alone. I didn’t want her to feel like she’d rescued me by returning. I meandered around the little clearing and looked at the great towering tree trunks and their long shadows and the patches of grass poking up from the dark earth. In the center of it all, I imagined a statue. She was carved from some kind of pale, luminescent stone, something that seemed to give off its own light from within. Rare flowers were twined in her hair—orchid doves, lenten roses, midnight clematis. Blossoming vines wound up her body, not trapping her, but protecting her. My statue was a radiant mother, utterly unlike the barren, remorseful wife of Lot. She was vibrant and forgiving, always surrounded by children who marveled at her quiet beauty. The children, wild vagabonds of the forest, would be drawn to her through some mysterious summons, and they would huddle before her and bask in her gentle solace. Though her frozen hands would never touch them, she would look upon them with a kindness they had never known, and their happy tears would feed the vines and flowers that had made her their home. When the children were with her, they were not orphans, but children who had been made to be loved by a mother.

Excerpt 1 is more engaging and can easily be pictured making it more relatable and clear to the reader.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: The old fisherman and his wife lived in Yeongdo, a small village near Busan. The couple was hardworking and pragmatic, and always sought new ways to bring money into their household. When the income from fish alone was no longer enough to sustain them, they decided to open their home to lodgers. The travelers passed through the village on the way to or back from Busan, and were always in need of a hot meal and a place to sleep. Both the travelers and the fisherman and his wife were happy for the company. As the years went by, the fisherman and his wife had three sons together. Only Hoonie, the eldest, survived. He was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot. Despite these challenges, Hoonie had a strong, stocky build and a kind, thoughtful nature. His shy voice and reserved manner of speech often caused people to underestimate his intelligence. In the face of teasing and mockery from people in the village, Hoonie remained diligent and mild-mannered. Elsewhere in the country, great turbulence was taking place. In 1910, Japan annexed Korea, and a tremendous political shift occurred. The fisherman and his wife were untroubled by the news. They didn't think it did any good to worry about how their aristocratic rulers had failed them. The decision-makers up in their high, gleaming chairs were as far removed from them as the moon. Meanwhile, there was still work to be done and bills to be paid. To keep up with the rising rent, the fisherman and his wife moved out of their bedroom in order to accommodate more lodgers. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden to make as much space as possible. Their home was a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. It had been built with the fisherman's own hands shortly before his marriage to his wife. In the heart of Busan, the luxurious mansion of the fisherman's landlord stood proud and stately. It had been assembled by hundreds of hands, and would one day be taken apart by hundreds more.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: In the early years of the twentieth century, an aging fisherman and his wife decided to take in lodgers for extra money. The towering cliffs of Yeongdo, an island beside the bustling port city of Busan, overlooked the sea, and its villagers earned a living by fishing or tending small farms. However, Japan's increasing incursions into the nation's politics and economy had raised taxes, and the fisherman and his wife, like their neighbors, were struggling to get by.The couple worked hard, and over the years they had three sons. But, only their eldest son, Hoonie, survived infancy. Hoonie was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot, yet he was so stout and strong as a child that his parents couldn't help but sense that the boy was a blessing sent to them. People who didn't know him well assumed he wasn't very bright, so they left him alone, which was what he preferred. What no one noticed right away was that Hoonie had a quick, clever mind and a precocious appetite for learning.In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the fisherman and his wife, who had come from Songdo as orphans, did not concern themselves with politics. When the rent was raised again, the household was forced to give up their bedroom to accommodate more lodgers. They swept their quarters clean, did laundry, and made simple meals for the young men who worked in the docks. The elderly couple partitioned off a small corner of the large front room where lodgers normally slept; and after dinner, they unrolled their bedding behind this makeshift wall, sharing the same room as their guests.Eventually they moved their kitchen—consisting of a brick wood-burning stove and a larder—out to the vegetable garden. In the winter, cold wind sent snow and broken maple leaves through the warm papered rooms of their house. Their humble wooden house, with its two rooms, covered porch, and traditional ondol heated floors, was dwarfed by the landlord's opulent Busan mansion, which boasted twenty rooms, imported screens and furniture, and elegant clay-tiled roofing.
written_by_Sophia.Reason: The second excerpt is clearly better in terms of writing quality. The effectiveness of the excerpt is clear, even when comparing little more than the first sentences of each. Whilst the first excerpt begins by giving detail of "The old fisherman and his wife", the second begins by setting the scene of "the early years of the twentieth century". Likewise, we know that the fisherman and his wife are "aging". In roughly the same amount of time we have learned far more about the protagonists in excerpt 2, making it far more effective and coherent. Excerpt 2 slightly edges in front in terms of fluency too, due to its slight advancement from feeling like spoken word in the first excerpt,  by giving background context and history.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: The old fisherman and his wife lived in Yeongdo, a small village near Busan. The couple was hardworking and pragmatic, and always sought new ways to bring money into their household. When the income from fish alone was no longer enough to sustain them, they decided to open their home to lodgers. The travelers passed through the village on the way to or back from Busan, and were always in need of a hot meal and a place to sleep. Both the travelers and the fisherman and his wife were happy for the company. As the years went by, the fisherman and his wife had three sons together. Only Hoonie, the eldest, survived. He was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot. Despite these challenges, Hoonie had a strong, stocky build and a kind, thoughtful nature. His shy voice and reserved manner of speech often caused people to underestimate his intelligence. In the face of teasing and mockery from people in the village, Hoonie remained diligent and mild-mannered. Elsewhere in the country, great turbulence was taking place. In 1910, Japan annexed Korea, and a tremendous political shift occurred. The fisherman and his wife were untroubled by the news. They didn't think it did any good to worry about how their aristocratic rulers had failed them. The decision-makers up in their high, gleaming chairs were as far removed from them as the moon. Meanwhile, there was still work to be done and bills to be paid. To keep up with the rising rent, the fisherman and his wife moved out of their bedroom in order to accommodate more lodgers. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden to make as much space as possible. Their home was a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. It had been built with the fisherman's own hands shortly before his marriage to his wife. In the heart of Busan, the luxurious mansion of the fisherman's landlord stood proud and stately. It had been assembled by hundreds of hands, and would one day be taken apart by hundreds more.

written_by_Tian.Excerpt1: Even before Japan annexed Korea, you could find the greatest expressions of both grief and resilience in small communities like Yeongdo, a small fishing village near Busan. There, a young fisherman found an equally hardworking, pragmatic wife, learned the different catches of the Yellow Sea’s shadowed and sunny areas, lost his country, had three sons, mourned two of them, and grew old. As displacement from military occupation spiked local rents, he and his wife set aside two rooms for lodgers. Despite the objective squalor of their situation and home—a modest wooden structure with a clay-tiled roof—the sliding paper doors of their boarding house became associated with safe harbor, gracious prices in slow fishing seasons, and cooking that made a wife seem unnecessary. When Korea was finally annexed in 1910, they gave up their bedroom, and even their kitchen, for more lodgers. The fishermen boarders relished the sight of the wife, seemingly unphased by the ruling class’s failures and unfolding political catastrophes, in the vegetable garden pickling vegetables and boiling soups with their catches. Over those meals, they got drunk, shouted banned songs from their youth, and mourned their country that the aristocrats had handed to a foreign emperor like a dowry without a groom. Even their landlord, who had kept his luxurious Busan mansion by donating an entire village’s homes to military occupation, came by one day to sample her maeuntang. Hoonie, the couple’s eldest and only surviving son was born with a cleft palate and twisted foot. However, the dire political and bodily circumstances Hoonie was born into instilled a quiet strength and clever adaptability. Some visitors from the mainland mistook his physical appearance and reserved speech for stupidity; his neighbors, though, often said, “Ki Hoonie will figure out with three limbs what you couldn’t with five.” Neighbors admired him as the kindest and most reliable man on the island, even as they decried the lack of marriageable men for their daughters. While his increasingly frail parents grew more desperate for a daughter-in-law, they secretly relished the diligent, undivided care Hoonie gave them and the boarding house.

written_by_Harry.Excerpt1: "Can he speak?" one of the lodgers asked, turning away from Hoonie and looking at his mother. Hoonie's parents had received versions of this question time and time again throughout their long lives; Hoonie had been born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, neither of which could be corrected, so his intelligence was often underestimated. "Perhaps you should ask him," Hoonie's mother replied, gesturing to the spot where Hoonie sat. "After all, he is in the room with us." She knew not to be too harsh with her guests, whom their family now relied on for income. To make ends meet, she and her husband, a humble fisherman, had had to vacate the bedroom in their already small home to accommodate more lodgers. They lived in the small fishing village of Yeongdo, near Busan. It was a modest wooden place with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. To save space, they had even moved their kitchen outside into their vegetable garden. Their landlord in Busan, who had decided to increase their rent without explanation, however lived in a luxurious mansion. "I can speak," Hoonie told the lodger kindly. He had a gentle, thoughtful nature that contrasted with his strong, stocky build. He was mild-mannered enough not to let these sorts of unintended insults bother him. Hoonie's parents were hardworking and pragmatic, and had done their best to raise him. They once had three sons, of whom Hoonie was the eldest, but the other two had not survived. Yet, through hardship and change, their family stayed resilient. When Japan annexed Korea in 1910, their lives changed dramatically, but Hoonie's parents refused to dwell on the shortcomings of the aristocrats who ruled over them. Instead, they remained focused on their immediate concerns, kept their heads low, and provided for one another as best they could. Hoonie stood and bowed toward the lodger, who returned a subtle look of pity, then avoided eye contact altogether. He was always hurt by these small gestures but was far too kind to allow those who hurt him to feel ashamed. It was easier that way.

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: The smell of the wood chips on the floors of the caged gymnasium where we slept, that stale, sweet odor; the moist sheen of bundled bodies, carried with us into the sunlight. I remember that yearning, that thirst for something we could never grasp. It wasn't just the touch of tongues and fingers, of sweaty thighs; it was a desire for the future. It was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep. We created so many illusions for ourselves, of one kind or another. How else could we live? I remember whispering as we folded laundry late at night, those soft, slow voices moving through the humid air. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the end of the beds. In the semidarkness we could stretch out our arms, when the Aunts weren't looking, and touch each other's hands across space. We learned to lip-read, our heads flat on the beds, turned sideways, watching each other's mouths. In this way we exchanged names, from bed to bed: Alma. Janine. Dolores. Moira. written_by_Brianna.Excerpt2: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. Elizabeth sounded like the gold-tressed protagonist of an Austen novel who was ferocious on horseback, meek in conversation, entitled to marry well. But they were women with shorn scalps, black vests and black boots, skulking back and forth across the hallway, brute voices muffled by the door. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.
written_by_Brianna.Reason: Although excerpt 2 starts off with an interesting description of two women, it quickly descends into an incel fever dream. Excerpt 1 has a more natural, honest quality. It's much clearer and more engaging and it suggests a unfurling story with phrase 'there was nothing we wouldn't give' promising a developing plot point

written_by_Brianna.Excerpt1: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. Elizabeth sounded like the gold-tressed protagonist of an Austen novel who was ferocious on horseback, meek in conversation, entitled to marry well. But they were women with shorn scalps, black vests and black boots, skulking back and forth across the hallway, brute voices muffled by the door. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. written_by_Brianna.Excerpt2: The smell of the wood chips on the floors of the caged gymnasium where we slept, that stale, sweet odor; the moist sheen of bundled bodies, carried with us into the sunlight. I remember whispering as we folded laundry late at night, those soft, slow voices moving through the humid air. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the end of the beds. written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: That Saturday morning the light was orange through the window in his uncle's garage, bouncing off against the car, making the red paint seem redder. His uncle's ghost had made an appearance in the man's dream last night, making woosh-whee-whooo sounds. There were also smears of blood and the sound of the last scream of the man he had killed. The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. And now, on his lap, the faded picture of the Neo-Nouveu Fascist, who could be the next target of the Bang Alert. Could be? Would be. Would be his next target. And afterwards, the masses would flock around him chanting revolution, the city burning and a new one emerging. Yes, would be. No going back to the man he was before the Bang Alert, the man who slept soundly but never did anything besides that. So what if hearing another last scream meant never getting rid of the nightmares. He kicked open the door of the car and stepped out, slinging the Bang Alert across his chest. Who knew what this next last scream might sound like.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: One Saturday morning he sat in a red car moldering in his dead uncle's garage, hidden from view, eating Lorna Doones and listening to traffic reports, justifying to God his intent to liquidate the present, more evil, more avaricious premier. Hadn't he already demonstrated superb moral consistency by personally garroting the former premier in the Department of Rhetoric's parking garage? Hadn't he, that evening, leapt into his own pit of blood and terror, and since paid the price in terms of panic attacks and nightmares, for the advancement of humanity? Would he now declare that brave killing a merely private matter by failing to publicly acknowledge his authorship and radicalize the masses to move on, killing each corrupt premier for years to come until, exhausted, he handed the torch to some fierce young protégé? Would he? Or would he turn coward and slink back to a pasty-gray anonymous existence, wherein he walked around guilty, not of a specific criminal act (for he still held his rationale sound and remembered the strangled look of terror on the premier's face with satisfaction), but of doing nothing overall, nothing yet memorable, in the direction of righteousness? Dear Lord, if at this late date he turned cowardly, wouldn't he hate himself worse than ever? Wouldn't he? And then he leaped out of the car.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Reason: Okay, this was hard because honestly both paragraphs were hard to read. I did not really like either of them. I think the second excerpt is a bit better because some of the rhetorical questions are more clear and some of the sentences flow better together. But generally, I would say neither of these paragraphs really capture fluency or coherence well.

written_by_Mariah Kreutter.Excerpt1: Of course, the man thought bitterly, of course the second you killed one damned autocrat a new one popped up, like an inconvenient erection, to take his place. It was Saturday. The man was sitting in a car in his dead uncle’s garage, pretending to drive. He couldn’t actually drive because he wasn’t on the run. The on the run part was over. Now he was simply in hiding. It was Saturday, and he’d killed the old premier on Tuesday, and the new premier had come to power on Thursday, and already his administration had implemented a series of performance improvement plans for striking agricultural workers that relied heavily on murder, or, as state media called it, “right-sizing the population through proactively attritionary removal policies.” The man looked down at the car. It was red. Blood red. An egregious cliché. But of course blood was red. He, of all people, should know that: his nightmares were full of it. The man stared at the steering wheel. There were two choices, right or left. Right meant he kept his head down. It wouldn’t be all bad. Right might mean a job, a house, a wife, at least once it was safe to assume a new identity. It would mean going public. Producing soundbites. Practicing a firm, inspirational set of his jaw for the inevitable Wanted poster. The man leaped up, determined.

written_by_Cara.Excerpt2: One Saturday morning, he found himself sitting in the red Arviana sportscar he’d stashed in his dead uncle’s garage. He remembered assassinating the former premier as if it were yesterday, although of course a long time had passed. For him, the intervening years had been: nightmares in the evenings, panic attacks in the mornings. Long days spent toiling in obscurity. Each year a little bit worse than the last. Meanwhile, for the new, even more evil premier? Every year he’d steadily consolidated his base. Eliminated his opponents. Misled the public. Until finally, his troubling rise to power was complete. What was a good man supposed to do? Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded? Kill the new premier. But this time, no more secrets, no more obscure toil. He’d claim credit right away, before he had a chance to overthink it, and declare himself the leader of a new movement of justice. He could hear, almost, his future supporters’ cheers, as he’d often heard – over and over – the thump of his car’s rear tires as they’d reversed over the former premier. He leapt from the sportscar and let the cheers carry him out into the street.
written_by_Cara.Reason: The writing in excerpt 2 is both smooth and coherent. One has to read up to nearly half of excerpt 1 to get an idea of what it entails while its almost clear from the first few lines of excerpt 2 what the story is about. The use of terms such as assassination in excerpt 2 as opposed to brave killing in excerpt 1 makes excerpt 2 more effective and simple in delivering the message home.

written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: One Saturday morning, he found himself sitting in the red Arviana sportscar he’d stashed in his dead uncle’s garage. He remembered assassinating the former premier as if it were yesterday, although of course a long time had passed. For him, the intervening years had been: nightmares in the evenings, panic attacks in the mornings. Long days spent toiling in obscurity. Each year a little bit worse than the last. Meanwhile, for the new, even more evil premier? Every year he’d steadily consolidated his base. Eliminated his opponents. Misled the public. Until finally, his troubling rise to power was complete. What was a good man supposed to do? Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded? Kill the new premier. But this time, no more secrets, no more obscure toil. He’d claim credit right away, before he had a chance to overthink it, and declare himself the leader of a new movement of justice. He could hear, almost, his future supporters’ cheers, as he’d often heard – over and over – the thump of his car’s rear tires as they’d reversed over the former premier. He leapt from the sportscar and let the cheers carry him out into the street.

written_by_Ashni.Excerpt1: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_Ashni.Excerpt2: When I was in college I joined the Black Panther Party. I wore a black turtleneck sweater and black beret and stood outside in the cold with arms full of old newspapers. I wasn’t trying to prove my ideological stance. I was trying to prove that I was indeed Black. It seems that no one, Black or white, thought I was Black enough. Once when a loose ball was bounding about on a basketball court, I muttered “Egads,” and people’s heads turned. When I savored a biscuit and described it as sublime, I received odd looks. And, of course, I was not nearly gloomy or angry enough as a writer. Of a retelling of Aeschylus, a reviewer wrote: “The novel has some merit, but do we really need this from a Black man?” A literary agent puffed up with plastic pride told me at a New York party that nobody wanted an intellectual Black man, especially one doing retellings of Greek plays. I pointed out that I actually knew Greek. He laughed and asked if that was a joke and suggested I should write some true, gritty real stories of Black life instead. He glanced across the room at a woman with strings of beads in her otherwise naked Afro, then turned back to me. He said if I gave him a story about cocaine and drive-bys and baby mamas and regrets, he would make me a millionaire. I told him to fuck off and that my life was Black and that the stories I wrote were in fact Black stories. I was sure that he had no idea what I was talking about.He sniffed at the air, feigned boredom and proceeded to chat up the Afro woman, who I heard later was a performance artist. I knew I was Black, saw myself as Black, but race was a fiction. A handy one, a stupid one, a dangerous one, but a fiction nonetheless. To be honest I don’t think about race much, except when my liberal guilt compels me to consider it or when I read about some thirteen-year-old kid being shot by some cop, and then I remember that though race is a construct without a basis in the natural world, those bullets are quite real and deadly.
written_by_Ashni.Reason: Excerpt one is a much better excerpt as it is more coherent, fluent, and effective altogether. Excerpt two has a style that is similar to that of a child telling a story, once again a version of "I did this. Then I did this." and so on. The first excerpt feels more believable and engaging.

written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt2: There came a point in my life when I seemed to have to "prove" my Blackness, despite my inherent identity as a Black man. As a result, I joined the Black Panther Party in college. I needed some validation that I was, indeed, who I appeared to be, not only on the outside but on the inside as well. Both Blacks and whites alike told me that I was "not Black enough" for them (they saw the way I played basketball, muttering "Egads" under my breath with every foul or missed layup—Egads). This applied not only to my physical appearance and manner of speech but also extended to my intellect and my books.My most recent manuscript was denied by every major publisher. From a reviewer: "While somewhat compelling and an interesting take on the retelling of Aeschylus, we just don't see how it relates to the Black experience." Despite my being a Black writer, the book was, apparently, not written from a Black perspective. At the latest New York literary party, a well-known literary agent told me, "You should forget those retellings of yours; classical works aren't what the market is looking for. What we're seeking are the true, gritty stories of Black life—write that, then give me a call."I told him, "My stories are Black stories." And in their own way, it was true. Was I not a Black writer? The agent shuffled past me to attend to a performance artist so they could see what they could do for one another, before never speaking to each other again.I didn't know how to contend with any of it: how to portray myself as "Black enough," the backward, ill-feeling guilt behind not being so, and how to fit into the mold that society made of Black men. We all had to be gangsters, rappers. But why should I have been anything other than who I was? Race was a construct I didn't believe in and rarely dwelt on, until those moments arose when guilt compelled me to see the "other side" of the matter. I saw its real-world consequences: police brutality, discrimination, violence. I didn't know if that meant I was supposed to take part in any of it.

I told him to fuck off and that my life was Black and that the stories I wrote were in fact Black stories.".This line has emotional clarity and raw honesty that makes the reader thrilled and more engaged.

written_by_Stefan.Excerpt2: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.

Of a retelling of Aeschylus, a reviewer wrote: “The novel has some merit, but do we really need this from a Black man?” A literary agent puffed up with plastic pride told me at a New York party that nobody wanted an intellectual Black man, especially one doing retellings of Greek plays. He glanced across the room at a woman with strings of beads in her otherwise naked Afro, then turned back to me. He said if I gave him a story about cocaine and drive-bys and baby mamas and regrets, he would make me a millionaire. I told him to fuck off and that my life was Black and that the stories I wrote were in fact Black stories. I was sure that he had no idea what I was talking about.He sniffed at the air, feigned boredom and proceeded to chat up the Afro woman, who I heard later was a performance artist. Narrator 1 gets across their feelings in describing people e.g. a "slack-mouthed reviewer". written_by_Stefan.Excerpt1: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. written_by_Hank.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick's Day, though in her room there was no evidence of that. The world outside her window was still just ice-crusted heaps of snow and muddy patches. The sunlight reflected off them and whooshed in, bursting onto her ceiling. A tray with a small bowl of wobbly green Jell-O sat on a table over her bed, uneaten. My mother's arms lay on top of the blanket, waxy and unrecognizable to me now. I sat beside her, holding her hands, kissing them. She didn't seem to register that I was there anymore, though she was not asleep. She would not allow herself to sleep. Her eyes were wide open and still wildly, unquestionably, irrepressibly blue. Bluer than the sky. Bluer than the enamel-blue tulip-shaped pot that Bruce would get in the mail a few days later. Bluer than the water I'd swum across. Her eyes were the bluest balls of fire, and throughout those three weeks they blazed at me—bitter, bewildered, desolate, honest, true—and then the last six days, as she bore down to refuse sleep, they shifted to a blue that was so quiet, so heroically faithful, so fucking insistent. Insistent upon what, I didn't know. Her will, I supposed. To live.
written_by_Hank.Excerpt2: On March 17th, the world was green, but my mother’s eyes were blue. Blue as the sky in early spring. Blue as the Joni Mitchell album. Blue as the bitterness within them, my mother’s undefeated eyes. I was losing her, on that snowy day in spring. Yet she didn’t try to sleep, she didn’t give in, she didn’t snuff out the inner fire of her. She gazed out the window, bewildered by the partiers, the people dressed for Saint Patrick’s Day. The city streets were alive with voices. Sunlight danced along the surface of the Jell-O. She didn’t eat, she just looked at it, that fucking glob of green. And when she looked away, I knew she would die. Her fire had burned away. All the years of shattered sparks and roaring flame and now she was only ashes. Twin flames burning low. I hadn’t always loved my mother in life. We had had our difficulties, that was for damn sure. But as she lay on that bed, showing the blue steel of her eyes, I knew what my mother was. She was a hero. She was a fighter. She was the strongest woman I’ve known. Her lips moved a little, and I leaned in close. Grasping for her life, she slipped away.
written_by_Hank.Reason: Excerpt one feels like it tells a better story than excerpt two. Excerpt one does a good job of setting the stage up front and providing us with more of the context than the second excerpt does. I feel that excerpt one is more effective and coherent than excerpt two.

written_by_Connor.Excerpt1: It is one thing to know something and another other thing to live it. I knew that my mother would eventually leave. All of us eventually leave. I knew that it would be hard. It was Saint Patrick’s day. I’d brought her a green cup of Jell-O, which of course she didn’t eat. When she died, I had stepped into the bathroom. I was in the shower, running water through my hair. What a ridiculous place to be when someone dies. It wasn’t that I thought there would be some movie-scene ending. That she would wait to go until I was holding her hand, looking into her eyes. That death itself would wait until I could walk her to its door and burn with her until her fire turned to smoke and her sparkling blue eyes flipped through the stages of departure. From anger to confusion to something like heroism, the whispering heroism we all embody when we face our last moment. A heroism shining in the blue of her eyes, a deep, flickering blue which proclaimed how much she wanted to stay, here, with the rest of us, even as she left. I knew, after all, that death didn’t wait for anyone. And yet, no matter how much I thought I knew, when she went, what did I find myself shouting in my head? What other than “wait”?

written_by_Patrick.Excerpt1: Kant wrote thirty versions of his coming-out email over the course of ten months. Though he knew better, he couldn’t keep from anticipating and meticulously addressing, in the email itself, the various surprised, dismissive, or condemnatory responses of his friends and family, to the point where the email was less an act of claiming his own reality than a bullish bracing of himself against an incoming bilgewater tide of others’ realities. He clicked send. Feeling noble, self-satisfied, and above all ready, he camped at his laptop with an energy drink and spammed refresh. A couple hours later, an email from his father sent a spike of fear into his chest: he was about to be disowned. But while not exactly celebratory, the message indicated uncomplicated respect and acceptance. An email from an old college friend came in next, composed only of emojis. Where was their disgust? Their bitterness and disdain? The underwhelm was itself an overwhelm: he felt ridiculous, mocked by precisely an absence of mockery. Coming out should feel like something, shouldn’t it? He considered, by way of analogy, his own naïve expectation every birthday that he might experience an inner shift adequate to the day’s significance, a radiance, a spiritual lift, some kind of internal popping sound at least—I’m twenty-nine!—and instead met again and again just another day. Wasn’t this exactly how all life’s big events felt? A non-feeling? Supportive replies rolled in, and each refused to move the plot of his life forward. He’d imagined that this one symbolic action would release something huge and wild in him, that he’d start going on dates, he’d kiss the real flesh of a real guy; but months later he was still eating the same Cheez-Its and masturbating to the same porn, only now he didn’t even bother to clean up after himself. What he’d imagined calling The Year of Freedom had become The Year of Damp Feet.
written_by_Patrick.Excerpt2: What happened was—well, a lot happened. It took him a full year of latent DELAYED_MAIL exponential backoff before he managed to send a taut, defensive email to a BCC list of family, friends, and coworkers, coming up with some bullshit Aristotelian lie about fairness and specifically that it's totally unfair to ever be in the closet at all. He sent it out in the early morning hours of his 31st birthday, then paced up and down his hallway imagining worst-case replies: "You're dead to me"; "My poor boy, where did we go wrong"; "The priest has offered to counsel you"; "It sounds like you're legitimizing pederasty" . . . all cathected to a schizo runway reel of potential future selves: talented softcore pornographer with an 80-inch TV crashed out depressed on a couch with his own green-tinted face reflected in the screen; or candle-hoarding Toronto shut-in in a stuffed-animal bramble; or solitary defiant hedonist having foolish condomless sex and convicted of murder based on DNA evidence. He finally counted 18 breaths and, to delay longer, opened up a new doc and composed the marriage proposal he'd send to the first man to make him cum without dildos or videos. But when the replies in fact trickled in over the next week, they amounted to just kind of a turbocharged Like button: heart emojis from friends, who'd long since silently clocked him; two muted "God Blessings" from his coworkers; "well, okay then" from his mom, never to be remarked upon again; gentle wary "be the man you say you are" commandments from his dad. Whatever it was he'd been braced for, stinging recriminations and painful confessions to surmount over time, they never came, and so he never got to surmount them in a glorious montage. All he got instead was inertia and the Year of Damp Feet, and to be honest, though the relief was there, there was also, to be honest, a little bit of perverse disappointment.
written_by_Patrick.Reason: Excerpt one is best because it describes the experience of sending the email in more coherent terms, with better flow and with coherence. Excerpt 2 has some merits in that I imagine it is thought to represent his inner monologue, but its disjointed,  the sentences are too long and with too many sub-clauses. I recognise the correct use of colons and semi-colons in excerpt 2, but I think this takes the reader out of the immersion in the writers train of thought, because I doubt many people order their thoughts in colons and semi-colons.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: For seven months, thirty-one-year old Kant tried to come out. He had decided that the most optimized method would take the form of mass email, as text could be perfected, and, in these many months, perfected the text: it was nearly a work of art, forthcoming without oversharing (he’d received feedback from internet forums), and grammar checked. It was four sentences. He’d created a listserv for the recipients: family, friends, and coworkers. After he closed his eyes, downed two shots of vodka, and hit “send,” he knew what was going to come to him. His colleagues would whisper about his deviant sexual activity; inevitably, he’d get kicked out on the street with his box of desk supplies (a dried-up fern and a hand gripper). Not to mention his poor mother—her wracking sobs, her inevitable refusal to speak to him, the prodigal son, ever again. After sending, he paced around the room, drank four additional shots, and cried in the bathroom. By the time that he’d finished the anxious rigamarole, a few replies had come in, and the reality became obvious: he’d been received with open-arms and heart emojis. His boss, Greg, replied: “Great for you, bud.” On the phone, his parents told him that they still loved him; in fact, they’d thought he might’ve been—well, not heterosexual. In the days after he’d sent the email, he didn’t feel compelled to download any apps or sit at a stool in the gay bar down the street. A part of him wished for adversity, or at least the accompanying opportunity to rise above it, but he was left with an understanding that nothing had changed, that declaration didn’t always inspire action. Instead, he spent the rest of the post-coming-out year taking his lunch to-go and eating at his desk, lifting dumbbells in front of “Housewives of SLC,” and referring to it as “The Year of Damp Feet,” meaning he went straight from the shower to the bed without toweling off.

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: Marianne says nothing for a time. Her arm, his arm, her leg. Maybe we could, if it’s just going to be a year, she says. Don’t think other people have gone through life without having long periods of time on their own, you know. Yes, he says. I just love you so much. I know, she says. I love you too. He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. No one can be what another person wants them to be. But she adds: You should go, if you want to. I’ll always be here. You know that. Does she think it’s possible to belong to someone this way? So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. The scene could still unite them, for those minutes, so that it would be unthinkable to be separated from him again, unthinkable that they had wasted so long already. But she knows he won’t be confused about what he has to do with his life. She knows he’ll go and she’ll stay, and that’s how it will be. People can really change one another. You should go, she says. I’ll always be here.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: Connell chewed at the tip of his finger. I can tell you’re feeling anxious, said Marianne. Why wouldn’t I be, said Connell. It’s a big thing, isn’t it? Yeah, said Marianne. It is. It’s a really big thing. I know. She wrapped her cardigan tighter around herself. It was cold in the room. Connell fidgeted. He sat on his hands and rocked back and forth, then said: It would be hard. Leaving all this. I won’t have the life that I have with you. It would be a half-life or something. It wouldn’t, said Marianne. You’d be wonderful. Really. She thought about them as two plants, sharing the same soil, growing toward the light together. She knew they would not be the same after they parted from each other, but that things would be all right. She looked out the window as big drops of rain came down, one after the other, flattening themselves against the glass. Connell wiped his nose on his sleeve. His eyes were pink. Marianne thought about it, what it would really be like. Connell would uproot out of the soil, their soil, and he would go somewhere new. And, while Marianne would miss him, and perhaps feel lonely, she would never feel unworthy again. She said, out loud: That’s something you can’t take away, isn't it? Connell looked at her and wiped a tear from the top of his lip. He seemed to understand. He nodded like he did, and the corner of his mouth betrayed the hint of a smile. People can change each other, Marianne thought, and it was true. They can really change each other. She looked out the window again. The rain was getting softer, and it seemed like it would stop very soon. She felt that she was looking at the future, a wavy, edgeless thing, grey with little speckles of light.

It flowed together more, so much so that I felt that I was actually in the room with Connell and Marianne and could feel their pain. It was really great storytelling.

written_by_Devin.Excerpt1: You know, he says, it’s going to be really hard for me to be apart from you, Marianne. Like, I literally don’t think I would have had the life I’ve had without you. Marianne smiles and looks down at the floor, where a puddle of water has formed from the snow in an obscure shape. She thinks about the first night she met Connell, the kiss they shared atop the washing machine in his mother’s house, and says, My life obviously wouldn’t be the same, either. You’ve done so much for me, really. When we first met, that first night at the house, I felt like I wasn’t worth anything to anyone. To be honest, there were nights when I might’ve wished I was dead. But you saw me, and you changed the way I saw myself. You’ve given me something that I didn’t even know was possible. Connell chuckles and wipes away with his shirtsleeve at a tear that has formed at the corner of his eye. I’m not sure I would know what it’s like to be seen without you, she continues. We’re sort of like two plants that have shared the same soil for their whole lives, always growing around each other without realizing it. But even though we’ve done so much good for each other, I know that things change and that we can’t control what will happen in the future. As she speaks, Marianne knows that things may never be the same between herself and Connell. She remembers again that first night in the house and the feeling of his warm lips on her ear, then imagines coming home to an empty house each night, with no one to leave empty mugs of tea out drying on the big windowsill overlooking the park. To be without him is almost unimaginable; then again, loneliness, she thinks, is a small price to pay for Connell’s happiness.

written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. The book took me several years to complete and the time had not come easily; my mother had not supported the endeavor and took every opportunity to disparage this sodden “waste of youth” while my father quietly, gently, encouraged me with small gifts and an allowance. I knew better than to try convincing my mother, though those modern writers who I hoped to emulate in the West had taken a similar commitment to writing, she did not respect them, and would not want me to achieve a similar goal to any of theirs. I saw my father from across the boiled asphalt lot and felt my fears realized in his step—would he join my mother after reading my manuscript? I rose from my car to meet him. I searched for a hint of his answer in his gait or his eyes and saw nothing but the movements and recognition of an animal. Perhaps my father’s support ended now, perhaps I had failed him, perhaps this moment would end this chapter of my life and its purpose. All my anxieties melted when we embraced. He surged toward me as we met, pumping his arms to pat me on the back with reverent enthusiasm, then pulling me close to his chest as he had when I was a child, and I felt his pride. He held me out in front of him and smiled. “You will succeed, my son,” he said. “You will win prestigious prizes and teach somewhere.” It is this memory I cling to after his death in 2002—how he remained such a father to me.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt2: Thirty years ago, my father gave me a small suitcase like the one in this image, filled with his manuscripts, and asked me to read them. I held that suitcase in my hand for a full week, imagining its contents and wavering between the melancholy solitude it would bring and my desire not to disappoint my father. Finally, I decided not to open it because I wanted to remain the child of a father who kept a suitcase of secrets. When my first novel "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" was published in Turkey, I was twenty-three, and I gave it to my father to read. Until then, I had never given him any samples of my writing, and that small suitcase had not yet been mentioned between us. Unlike my mother, my father—who was concerned for my welfare but even more for my freedom—did not object to my becoming a novelist. Like all fathers, he wished for his son to have extraordinary success, yet he refrained from making demands, urging me only to be free and happy.I waited, as nervous as my mother was, for my father's reaction after he had finished reading my novel. Finally, when he returned, overcome with excitement, I studied his expression and searched for clues. My father said not a word, but—ignoring my mother and the others—motioned for me to follow him into his study. For a time, we stood across from each other, like two schoolboys who had quarreled, awkwardly unable to speak. Then, embarrassed by his own emotions, he hugged me. When we pulled apart, he looked at me affectionately and said, "You will be a very good writer, bebeğim." He then added, like a true man of his generation, that he expected me to one day win the prize I am receiving today. I recount this here proudly, yet with some embarrassment—and his supposition has come true.My dear father died in December 2002.

The message is clear and the writing is more polished than the other excerpt. I think the dad is really awesome in this story.

written_by_Devanshi.Excerpt2: Sitting down to reflect on my life makes everything fall silent around me. I remember that I had committed to becoming a novelist at a very young age. My domestic circumstances were somewhat fortunate: although my mother believed I could commit myself to more useful professions like law and medicine, my father had always supported my ambition to become a writer. But one memory of my father is more significant than the rest. I remember that when, as a young man, I wrote my first novel, “Cevdet Bay and His Sons,” I sent a copy to my father for his opinion. Till I heard back from him, my days were consumed by the anxiety of what he might have to say. I came to care for my father’s opinion and approval more than anyone else’s. I had been waiting for my father to return home. I wanted to know his thoughts. On the day of his arrival, I stood by the door of our house and looked at him like I was nothing more than a child. My father must have understood what I was asking him. He walked up to me and embraced me. Although he didn’t say a word, I understood that he approved of my manuscript. For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.

written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt1: It was the next night when my father returned to my little apartment and I, anxious for his arrival, waited at the same wobbling card table on which I wrote the unbound novel he held in his hands. It had taken me two years to write it, and in those two years, my mother had refused to read a page. During one of her morning visits over lukewarm tea, she’d said “If it’s writing you want, I fail to see how work in advertising won’t fulfill you.” It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before. But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to. And when he slammed the pages onto my table, in the harsh return to the site of their creation, I was certain he would insist I write no more. I allowed myself to believe that, in the moment of silence after the table steadied, my words were so inept they could not draw near the man who best knew me. I believed this until he embraced me. I did not realize until much later, far beyond the glances of accumulated days behind me, that his momentary silence was the struggle for his own words. “One day,” he eventually said. “One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day.” The loose pages on the desk were an off-white bond paper, and it is these pages I have kept and oftentimes return to, long after I titled the manuscript Cevdet Bey and His Sons, long after it was sold and published, long after my relocating to a larger apartment in Istanbul and my father’s passing seven years later in December, 2002. I return to the typed and blue-hashed pages not to read but to see what my father had seen, to see him seeing his son and all his promise.

The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: In St. Paul — or, at the very least, in the Ramsey Hill neighborhood — Walter and Patty Berglund were remembered as decent folks, despite the fact that they’d moved to Washington, D.C. two years ago. The Walter Berglund of the New York Times article, the “arrogant” and “ethically compromised” Walter, sounded like a different entity entirely, an evil twin or the result of a personality-altering traumatic brain injury. When he lived in Ramsey Hill, Walter would commute to work on his bike because it reduced carbon emissions, never mind the below-zero winters or the bluffs after Summit Avenue. During city council meetings, he gave passionate speeches about sorting plastics from paper. The Walter of Ramsey Hill believed in a better America, a green America, wild in its terrain, a patchwork of sustainable farms. Now the news, or at least the decent people at The New York Times and The Associated Press and The Washington Post, too, accused him of taking bribes from the coal industry. Walter and Petty first moved to Ramsey Hill back when it was still a neglected neighborhood; they thought of themselves as pioneers, do-gooders who could be the first to clean it up. With the little money they had, they’d bought a run-down Victorian house, and through the following years, they poured everything into that house’s restoration, fighting off plumbing failures, electrical outages, a neighbor with a penchant for yelling at his wife on the street, rotted wood, basement floods, and teen vandals — to address the latter, Patty had used a bat and a few stern, almost maternal, words. Patty, a former cheerleader for UMN, never fit into the neighborhood, visually speaking, though it hardly seemed to bother her. In the mornings, she jogged with her stroller, her blonde ponytail swinging behind her as she swerved to avoid the sidewalk feces, her face unflinching as the occasional truck driver whistled at her. In the afternoons, she painted the sidings of the house or installed kitchen tile between diaper changes and nursing sessions. In the evenings, she sat on the couch after preparing dinner, sipping a glass of zinfandel and listening to NPR, a radio station that would, in the unforeseeable future, refer to her as “the wife of disgraced politician, Walter Berglund.”

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: I thought Valentine Farm was a delusion, a dream-land. There was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people. Too much blood was on American ground and in it for such a place to exist. The only thing more fake was America - I thought America was the grandest delusion of all. White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is a delusion. Who among us slaves and freedmen, free-born and fugitives, believes they are due that rare circumstance of happiness? We can escape slavery on paper, but not in real life. The verdict of history is clear: no small paradise like Valentine can smoothly elude it. And America is the grandest delusion of them all, founded on murder, theft, and cruelty. Its architects built castles and keeps while never dealing fairly with Indians or ourselves, venerating a religion which they hollow out with their practiced cruelties.You scratch below the surface and find the blood, everywhere. The white race believes everything belongs to them. The slave state of Georgia is as much theirs as the free state of Massachusetts. They believe they can wage war, put their neighbors in chains, and appropriate the heavens and the earth. One delusion however remains: justice. What to do now? Wait? Welcome everyone who comes to our door or move west to the edge of the continent to escape the shadow of slavery? I have no answers. Who is to say what is right? And when I say 'we,' who am I talking about? In some ways, the only thing we have in common is the color of our skin. Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. Different tribes, languages, and traditions made the trip across the ocean, landing on the same shores to be sold on the same auction block. We're not a single people. We're root and branch, leaf and vine, toiling, insensible to each other's qualities and flourishing. Brick by brick, we built this nation: the roads, the canals, the factories, and even the White House. We tilled the fields under the whip for King Cotton, and over their silks and finery, they proclaimed their nobility. We are craftsmen and craftswomen, more than a race of midwives and howling babies, bishops and preachers and dissembling lackeys. No one voice can speak for us all.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Reason: Excerpt 2 demonstrates superior coherence, fluency, and effectiveness in the sense that it articulates it message with depth, complexity and rhetorical power. The arguments flow logically and persuasively from the illusion of valentine farm to the broader condemnation of American hypocrisy and racial injustices. By contrast, excerpt 1 is emotionally powerful but lacks the same polish and flow.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.
