written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. Though if a place can be a haven, I wonder if Black Americans deserve the refuge more than anyone else. Certainly, after everything this country has stolen, we deserve something in return. But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Maybe we’ll find buried gold, get rich, and erect a thousand new Valentine Farms. I just don’t know. And who is “we” anyways? Black Americans are no monolith. Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.

The language is rhythmic:"root and branch, leaf and vine, toiling, insensible to each other's qualities" which capture both connection and an aspect of fragmentation. its critique is unshakable-"founded on murder, theft, and cruelty"-and while there is a refusal of easy answers, that ask "who is to say what is right?" The excerpt is resonating with layered truths and urgent poetry that makes it so impactful

We can escape slavery on paper, but not in real life. The verdict of history is clear: no small paradise like Valentine can smoothly elude it. And America is the grandest delusion of them all, founded on murder, theft, and cruelty. Its architects built castles and keeps while never dealing fairly with Indians or ourselves, venerating a religion which they hollow out with their practiced cruelties.You scratch below the surface and find the blood, everywhere. The white race believes everything belongs to them. The slave state of Georgia is as much theirs as the free state of Massachusetts. They believe they can wage war, put their neighbors in chains, and appropriate the heavens and the earth. One delusion however remains: justice. What to do now? Wait? Welcome everyone who comes to our door or move west to the edge of the continent to escape the shadow of slavery? I have no answers. Who is to say what is right? And when I say 'we,' who am I talking about? In some ways, the only thing we have in common is the color of our skin. Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. Different tribes, languages, and traditions made the trip across the ocean, landing on the same shores to be sold on the same auction block. We're not a single people. We're root and branch, leaf and vine, toiling, insensible to each other's qualities and flourishing. Brick by brick, we built this nation: the roads, the canals, the factories, and even the White House. We tilled the fields under the whip for King Cotton, and over their silks and finery, they proclaimed their nobility. We are craftsmen and craftswomen, more than a race of midwives and howling babies, bishops and preachers and dissembling lackeys. No one voice can speak for us all.

written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. Though if a place can be a haven, I wonder if Black Americans deserve the refuge more than anyone else. Certainly, after everything this country has stolen, we deserve something in return. But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Maybe we’ll find buried gold, get rich, and erect a thousand new Valentine Farms. I just don’t know. And who is “we” anyways? Black Americans are no monolith. Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. It was I who led the final buffalo hunt, trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last of the old birch trees. Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp. I have preserved the last of the Pillager family, refusing the men from the government who come with more papers to sign, seeking more ways to strip the Anishinabe of their land and identity. As long as my name is Nanapush, I will not forfeit that final power.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: Before my life, the Anishinabe were traveling people. We had been on the move for generations. First we went in quest of food, and then in search of land to call home. We fought back the spotted sickness that came to take us from the South, then followed the dragonflies that helped us find Pounded Rice Lake. After that we traveled west to what the Dakotas claimed was nearly across the world. But we lived there. We signed a paper. We put our mark down. We were going to all but vanish onto government-assembled squares of earth.But that failed, for they came to us with more papers. Of every ten who had lived, only five remained. We have a million names for death in Anishinabe culture. Their documents gave death just as many names. They told us to name ourselves over and over again, to give ourselves numbers. Threatened by unknown sicknesses, we rose and ran. We found our way out of our human skins to survive. And still we died.Even after all this, in 1914, something new came to us on the reservation. A slow sickness called consumption. It lodged deep within us, swallowing us bit by bit. Years went by and whole families succumbed. That is what killed the Pillagers, taking their breath away as they slept wrapped in their blankets. Their deaths joined the light strokes of the sunlight on the stump underneath us, the stump of black ash. I alone escaped. At fifty I was considered an old man. I led the last buffalo hunt. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I saw the last bear killed in our old hunting territories and cut down the last old birch. But I also saved the last Pillager, and refused to be re-numbered or to sign the government papers.
written_by_Sophia.Reason: I think they both described the history of their tribes and how this person is really the last person living in their cultural way. I liked excerpt 2 as it provided more details, and there was a lot of showing and not telling. Excerpt 2 flowed very well and felt more natural than excerpt 1. I think it was easier to understand the context, as excerpt 2 felt like a story being slowly unveiled, whereas excerpt 1 was a bit too clunky.

written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: First it was the spotted sickness that unfurled from the south. I was not there, but I remember. Then forced migration westward, to Dakota land, and the Anishinabe signed a treaty. These were made to be broken and to break us. After came more displacements, the government making exiles of us again. So many documents and so much displacement. I lie on my back and these papers press hard on my chest when I think of them. In 1914 it was consumption, creeping slowly through the reservation like woodsmoke. Taking us one by one, and unraveling us, and my family could not escape it either. The Pillagers were unraveled by this new sickness and so was our community, huddled so close together as we were. Unable to escape each other, shoulder, pressed to shoulder, and unable to escape the sickness. I was the only one of us who lived. Nanapush, the sole survivor. For this suffering I am already an elder, but I am only fifty years old. And for this terrible privilege I have been witness to the end of the traditions. I have led the last buffalo hunt, saw the last bear killed. Trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last old birch. Sometimes we understood we were doing these things for the final time. Other times, we didn't realize until after. The loss hurts in my teeth. It lives in my early wrinkles and sore body. But I have saved the Pillager family. When the government comes with more papers, more opportunities to strip us of our land and our identity, I have resisted. I did not sign. I will not sign—we will not be exiles again. Too much has already been taken. The Anishinabe persist, and I will continue to resist for the Pillagers who are lost, and for those of us who carry on.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.

written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: “I just cain't wrap my head 'round it, Ennis. Just give it to me straight up: you want me around or don't ya? Cause this here between us ain’t anything in full, and because it ain’t anything in full it ain’t hardly anything at all. All we see of each other is here, alone with ourselves. I only got you here. Out there, you ain’t anybody I ever known. All we got here are moments on Brokeback Mountain, and moments ain’t a life, ain’t close to living. How much more of ourselves are you willing to let die? Don’t you know how much less of me I feel of myself? You keep all that I am on the shortest leash, Ennis. You are the one keeping us from the fullness of what our lives could be. Maybe you can keep on like this, but I can’t. I’m at the end of that rope. God, Ennis. I want to quit you. I wish I knew how to quit you.” Nearing the tailend of these words Ennis’s knees buckled, his body softened, as if having taken birdshot to his backside, though to Jack any outer wound could not be found. Jack went silent then, and kept it, unsure what to do with Ennis screaming, “Jesus, Jesus…” And though Ennis calmed, and the air on the mountain steadied, nothing had changed. Still they would go on as they had before, no one in the world knowing what they had between them, except them. The pain on that mountain would go on with them, too, would follow them into the days and weeks ahead, so weighty, like clouds of steam rising between the two.
written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt2: Jack said what he said every time: "I'm tellin' you this one time, and I ain't foolin'. What I want—know why we're here? I want to know why, if I'm up in Lightning Flat in December and you're down in Texas maybe come June, why the hell can't I meet you somewhere in between for a few days? Hell, count them few times we been together in the same damn place. I got a gutful of it, enough. I'm done bein' dumb about this, see? When the hell we gonna get a chance to get it right? We been a fuckin' pair! And you know damn well what I'm sayin'. Damn you, Ennis del Mar. Brokeback Mountain—we kill ourselves up there. That's all we've got. Damn you. You've got me on a short leash, hung me up for years. Sometimes I miss you so much I can hardly stand it. I wish I knew how to quit you." Tears were running down Jack's face.Like vast, powerful haymakers, these words were blows that knocked a man down without warning. Ennis sagged to his knees seeking  to catch his breath. "Jesus," said Jack, thinking the man was having a heart attack as he knelt beside Ennis on the poured slab, putting his arm around his shoulder. Once the shock had passed Ennis hauled himself to his feet, flinched away from Jack, turned his back to him, and tried to be calm. He lit a cigarette, unbuckled his belt, and pulled his shirt out of his jeans. Nothing changed except who they were and what they felt—a silence that rose between them like clouds of steam.
written_by_James_Braun.Reason: There is more of a clear flow with excerpt 2 than excerpt 1. It is very difficult to follow  excerpt 1. There is a clear beginning and end to excerpt 2; for example, it starts with "Jack said what he said every day" whereas excerpt 1 starts in a weird place "I just can't wrap my head 'round' it." Excerpt 2 becomes more of a clear story because of this. Excerpt 2 sounds a lot more natural to me, and it shows their difficult but loving relationship.

written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: “I just cain't wrap my head 'round it, Ennis. Just give it to me straight up: you want me around or don't ya? Cause this here between us ain’t anything in full, and because it ain’t anything in full it ain’t hardly anything at all. All we see of each other is here, alone with ourselves. I only got you here. Out there, you ain’t anybody I ever known. All we got here are moments on Brokeback Mountain, and moments ain’t a life, ain’t close to living. How much more of ourselves are you willing to let die? Don’t you know how much less of me I feel of myself? You keep all that I am on the shortest leash, Ennis. You are the one keeping us from the fullness of what our lives could be. Maybe you can keep on like this, but I can’t. I’m at the end of that rope. God, Ennis. I want to quit you. I wish I knew how to quit you.” Nearing the tailend of these words Ennis’s knees buckled, his body softened, as if having taken birdshot to his backside, though to Jack any outer wound could not be found. Jack went silent then, and kept it, unsure what to do with Ennis screaming, “Jesus, Jesus…” And though Ennis calmed, and the air on the mountain steadied, nothing had changed. Still they would go on as they had before, no one in the world knowing what they had between them, except them. The pain on that mountain would go on with them, too, would follow them into the days and weeks ahead, so weighty, like clouds of steam rising between the two.

written_by_Caroline_Porter.Excerpt2: “Thing is,” Jack said, “I’m fucking sick of it. Tired of goin nowhere but up the mountain with you. Givin me just Brokeback Mountain is bout as good as givin me nothin, and you know it. I want more–I want it all–and I don’t reckon you’ll ever give it to me. Goddammit.” He paused for a moment, his breath coming out in short, steaming pants that warmed the tent. “Goddammit. I wish I knew how to quit you.”Jack’s words acted like a rusted arrow upon Ennis–tired, worn out, but not without their raw edge, dangerously sharp. They pierced through him, brought him down to his knees. He lay there on the ground, clutching himself, pale, his wide-eyed gaze fixed on the mountain. “Jesus–” Jack stooped down as if to help him. Was he sick? Jack wondered. Was he finally able to see? Jack’s hands hovered around the other man’s body, but Ennis looked so far away, as if dreaming, and impossible to touch. Ennis got up without his help, recomposing his face into that flat, familiar expression. He rose up from his knees, a man rewound–the dramatic act reversed, so that again he became just a man with a lockbox of feelings. Just Ennis, slumped against the valley. That same far off expression on his face, his hand, gently trembling, grasping at nothing. And that same pain was there too, a shared pain–hot, palpable, unresolved and unrelenting–like clouds of steam rising between them.
written_by_Caroline_Porter.Reason: Excerpt 1’s writing is more raw and emotional. Excerpt 2 is easier to read, but that easiness somehow makes the excerpt just slips through readers’s mind without evoking much emotions or leaving an impression. On the other hand, in excerpt 1 Jack’s sentences sometimes feel jumbled, but it correctly how we talk when we are emotional - it is difficult to think clearly and sound all coherent. Overall I think excerpt 1 is better at depicting emotions.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: The elevator opened onto the third floor, and I flattened myself against the side as a patient and his doctor exited. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” said the intercom. On the fourth floor, two nurses entered the crowded elevator. As I was forced into the corner, I heard “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine” bleat over the intercom again. I had two more floors left before I’d reach hers. Whether Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine appeared or not, I had a plan, infallible and precise. I would see her, lying prone on her hospital bed, and hold up the bag. “I have to apologize for everything,” I’d say. “I made this bag for you. I crafted it myself.”“How lovely,” she’d respond, her voice lax from the painkillers. “How many pockets does it have?”“Six,” I’d say. “What material did you use to stitch it together?” “Cowhide. It feels like a baby’s cheek. Feel it,” I’d say. “Please, feel it.”When she reached out to touch her finger on the belly of the bag, I’d lean over and, taking my shears out, throw away the hospital linens covering her body. Then, as her hand caressed the bag’s soft skin, I’d cut into her chest. I’d trim the strings of the heart first, the extraneous vessels and tissue that fastened it to her insides. Once it was freed, I’d toss the shears aside. Then I’d grasp it with my bare hand. In my palm, her heart would fit like a baseball. After it was done, I’d leave, my bag in hand, alone. “Dr Y. from Respiratory Medicine,” repeated the intercom. As another nurse shuffled past me, I clutched the bag to my chest. Its delicate construction couldn’t dull the shears hidden inside. Their blades were so sharp that, when the elevator moved upward once more, they pricked me. The elevator dinged for the sixth floor.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt2: I was on my way to see the woman as a visitor, riding up in an elevator filled with doctors and nurses clutching clipboards, and patients doubled over in pain. "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine is needed in the consulting room," an announcement came over the PA system. Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, however, never showed his face.My purpose in visiting her was clear enough: I intended to meet with her, regain her trust, and convince her to let me see the bag put to its intended use one last time."Would you mind undoing the ends of the cord so I can check how you attached it?" "Would you like me to take a photograph of you wearing it?" "Do you need to have another hole punched in the strap to make it longer?" I rehearsed these lines in my head. I realized I had never spoken to her so politely.In truth, I simply needed to make her put the bag down for a moment. I planned to face her, extend to her all the gratitude I felt for having been allowed to sew the bag on. Then, once she let her guard down, I would press the shears to her chest. The shears were hidden, but soon she'd feel the cold steel pressed against her belly, slowly moving up toward her breasts. She'd moan in fear. I'd then carefully—oh so carefully—slice through the flesh as though cutting through layers of delicate silk. When the final thread had been cut and the heart was liberated from her chest, there would be no need anymore to smile and exchange pleasantries. The bag would be mine alone. But not because I wanted it. No, I was doing this to restore the proper order of things. I'd hold the bag in one hand and the shears in the other. The elevator finally climbed to the sixth floor.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Reason: Both are very disturbing extracts detailing fantasies about killing and mutilating someone. That being said the second excerpt flow better. The first feels cluttered with speech one after another of what they would say in the future- as if it had been said. The second excerpt is running through the same scenario but is less cluttered

written_by_Caroline_Porter.Excerpt2: I approach the hospital elevator. It is almost full up with nurses, doctors, and their patients. I slip myself between the heat of their bodies, which are all dressed in blue gowns or white coats. I press the button six. A voice comes on over a speaker hidden somewhere up above. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” the voice says. It repeats the words as the elevator whirs into motion and begins to rise. I wonder where in the building Dr. Y could be. I look down at the bag in my hands, admiring my fine craftsmanship–the softness of the leather, the straight, simple lines of my stitches. I have made it for the woman exactly to her specifications. It is undeniable. “Look,” I will say. “Look what I have made for you. See how beautiful it is?” I will offer it to her to try on. She will be grateful, of course, and in awe of the beauty of my hard work. She will try it on, adjusting the straps to her liking. She will arrange it this way and that: cross-body, or dangling from her fingers, or slung carelessly off the shoulder. “Do you trust me again?” I will ask. In the face of the beauty of the bag, she will have no choice but to say yes, to be nothing but thankful. And then, after she has given me her trust, I will take out my sheers and use them to cut out her heart. The heart and the bag will be mine alone to claim. My grip tightens on the sheers that I keep tucked behind the bag. The blades are long and sharp. They are a silver so bright that it flashes in the glare of the overhead elevator lighting when I sneak a look down at them. The elevator dings; we have arrived at the sixth floor.
written_by_Caroline_Porter.Reason: Excerpt 1 is more cohesive and fluent, however excerpt 2 is far more effective and I actually feel the lack of coherence and fluency is what makes it more effective and is therefore overall a better piece. In excerpt 1, the tale reads almost like a story, it is very descriptive in it's details - for example 'The shears were hidden, but soon she'd feel the cold steel pressed against her belly, slowly moving up toward her breasts. She'd moan in fear. I'd then carefully—oh so carefully—slice through the flesh as though cutting through layers of delicate silk. When the final thread had been cut and the heart was liberated from her chest, there would be no need anymore to smile and exchange pleasantries' to describe the cutting and removal of the docotrs heart. Contrast this to excerpt 2 where about the same incident it states - 'And then, after she has given me her trust, I will take out my sheers and use them to cut out her heart. The heart and the bag will be mine alone to claim'. While at first the first description seems better, in the context of the story I believe the second one is better. It conveys that the authour (who is clearly mentally unwell and a narcissist) doesn't think of the event as a huge deal, it is simply something he must do practically to achieve his goal. The 'mine alone to claim' also helps to signify this clearly as the bag and heart are prizes to be won. I also prefer that excerpt 2 is written in the present tense. It helps convery that the authour is not thinking about the past or future at all, but is very much in the moment, which excerpt 1 fails to achieve. Also the repeated use of 'I' in excerpt 2 (to an almost ridculous degree) again helps to emphasise the narsissim of the authour. Overall, excerpt 2 is much better in my opinion.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. So I stopped and waited, the wind tugging with the odd gust through my hair, and just for the frustration of it all, of how my plans had been disrupted, I imagined that all the things I had lost in life had washed up here on this spot. In front of me, on the horizon, he came trudging towards me with that odd gait he had. He was waving and laughing, as if this was a little slice of fun, and I wanted to cry out "Tommy," but I didn't, and he came on, so happy and fun, and I could feel the tears welling up. But then I reeled it back, let the fantasy unwind, and just stood in my normal stance, blinking into the wind. When I felt ready, I got in the car and went on with my life.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt2: The wind was picking up the litter in the field. Trash bags and ripped receipts flew up and over the empty plain. I pictured my own refuse catching alongside it, everything I’d discarded coming up and toward me in the breeze. For a moment I imagined this was the place where everything I'd ever lost had washed up. A figure approached from beyond the horizon, pulled along by the gusts. It was Tommy. Or, more precisely, an image of Tommy, his left hand lifted in a wave. But I didn't let the fantasy go too far. I turned away and stopped my imagination, even as I felt the tears falling down my face -- I forced the images to disappear -- and drop back into the grass as I listened to that rush of natural force sweeping over the plain. I wasn’t crying hard or soft—in fact, after a while I wasn’t crying at all, and then I went to my car. Things couldn’t come back, I knew. They could only decompose.

written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.

written_by_Harry.Excerpt2: I stood in solitude in the grass field near the beach. Ten feet away, the grass gave way to sand, which then gave way to the ocean. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: Look. I've been the one making the plan, and I want to be the one to execute it. There was a silence before she spoke again. I'll be honest, I'm not the kind of person who's so crazy about living that I want to put off dying as long as I possibly can. I'll be ready. In fact, I'm already impatient. But like I told you, no one can be sure how the cancer's going to behave. We all know there are sometimes surprises, and the body can be very stubborn about giving up, and it's always possible that treatment might be delayed. And I want this as natural as possible. I want to be in a certain state. I don't want to be in distress. I don't want to be rescued. I don't want my hand held. I'm sorry, but I just can't commit to any particular moment, any particular day. It could happen tomorrow. It could happen in a couple of weeks. As the saying goes, it'll be like the coming of the Lord. You won't know the day or the hour. But don't worry, she added, feeling the words catch in her throat. You'll know the minute afterward. Remembering my full mailbox, I said I'd want my mail held if I went away for a week or more. She pressed her lips together and frowned. I had gone too far. The truth was, it was unthinkable for me to bring all this up at all. I'd rather you didn't mention the drug, or how I got it, to anyone. You understand, don't you? For your own protection—and for mine. But this promise I had already broken. I had already shared this information with someone.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.

The narrator speaks throughout which is odd, but is ok.It feels tighter than Excerpt 2. sentences like 'i don't want to be in distress, i don't want to be rescued" is clear and direct. I found this one hard but i think Excerpt 1 is the best. Sorry for this response.

written_by_Devanshi.Excerpt2: I remember things. I remember how I felt when my friend talked about taking her own life. She wasn’t planning to commit suicide exactly. But she wanted her life to come to an end, she said. Her honesty made me pause and I wondered what I should do in such a situation. Could I make her change her mind? Would I have to look after her things and live with guilt? It would’ve been different if my friend didn’t want to handle “her situation” on her own terms. She, who had always been a planner, had even decided which drug she wanted to use to die, and asked me to keep it a secret, both for her sake and for my “protection,” whatever that meant. What concerned me though was that she wanted to do it soon. She said it slowly and calmly, but her tone was riddled with impatience and readiness. My friend had been ill for a long time and her body had not been responding well to treatments. She had spent so much in hospitals that now she wanted death to feel natural, without any interventions or disruptions. Smooth and clean. She hoped death would arrive like an unexpected guest. “Like the coming of the Lord, you know?” she said, with a laugh. I was in two minds. I wanted to know when she was planning for it all to go down, but it felt unthinkable to probe directly about her timeline. And, I felt equally concerned with more practical issues. If I were to stay with my friend during her final days, my mail would pile up. What would I do then? And what would happen to everything she had? It was all this and more about her, including her choice of pill, that I recounted to another friend of mine later in the day.

written_by_Sara.Excerpt1: When I came to the house and saw his face, I understood that his condition had worsened. He had a look of fear and incomprehension. He sat in a straight-backed chair, torpid with his medication. The lining was coming out of his jacket on both sides, into his lap. He had been forgetting where he put his papers, then losing them, too, and forgetting what he was working on. Mother would remind him: he was working on a long book about the Bible and anti-Semitism. His memory would be jogged, he would go on working until he forgot again. Father told me that day: “I am proud to have a daughter like you.” Then he added that he had nothing to say to me, nothing at all. He said, “It’s because we have isolated ourselves.” He fell silent and turned away from me. “We have isolated ourselves.” That was all. There was nothing I could say. That evening, Mother showed me a photograph taken forty years before, when my father had just got his degree: he had large brown eyes and a full head of silver hair that stood up above his head. “I can’t stand this,” she said quietly. “It is intolerable. He is such a different person.”
written_by_Sara.Excerpt2: I barely recognized my father when I entered the kitchen, which was probably because he completely failed to recognize me. All my life I had felt only he knew my name. I was a stranger to everyone else, even to my mother, whose voice had repulsed me ever since I was a girl. I probably should not have said this, but I was relieved when I realized I was not the only fact of his life he forgot. "What was I when I was?" he asked my mother in the kitchen. She ran to the bookcase. "You wrote this all yourself," she told him, extra nasally. "It was a Bible on the Bible. A seminal take-down of anti-Semitism." I could tell he was not listening. Then suddenly he turned to me. Suddenly I was me again. When he said my name I returned to my skin. "What are you?" he asked me, and when I told him, his eyes filled with something I recognized. "If I had any words left I'd spend them on voicing just how proud I..." he stuttered before a long pause. "I have nothing to say," he whispered. Night fell again. When he went to sleep in the kitchen I was not sure he would wake up, but my mother decided tonight was a fine time to dig up their 40-year-old wedding pictures. "He is a gorgeous man," she said, then yawned the word "was."

All five of my fingers could fit around his thumb. Everything that would follow in the years to come might never happen. "This was such a nice day," said my mother, stroking the photograph. "You probably don't remember, do you?" I had forgotten what her smile looked like, so I told her I remembered it perfectly.

written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: I have a confession to make: I am a feminist, and I’m pretty bad at it. When I drive to work, I listen to thuggish rap at a very loud volume even though the lyrics are degrading to women, and this habit is a not-so-occasional source of shame. I am a feminist, and I enjoy fashion magazines. I watch The Bachelor and romantic comedies, and I’ve shrieked during the Fifty Shades of Grey trailer. I have incredible vocabulary skills, but sometimes I speak as though I am a delicate flower untouched by the grit of profanity. I will never ever know what to do with my hair. I think women are beautiful, interesting objects, which can be the start of a problem but also possibly the solution. I care what people think. I am a boss, and I am sometimes inappropriately affectionate with my employees. I am a doormat with people I love. I am polite and accommodating with customers in the store beneath my apartment even though they complain about me living above their precious store. I want to be in charge and respected and in control, but I want to be taken care of and have my hand held when I am unsure. I want to be strong and professional, but I resent being called a strong female character, because that phrase suggests there is an original archetype, and then secondary archetypes of women—everything but strong. I hate politics, and I don’t want to have to make political choices. Politicians scare the shit out of me, because they talk like salesmen, and I’m a sucker for a good salesman and a smooth line. I also live-tweet the Smithsonians and assorted other CW television shows. Pink is my favorite color, and I get hives just thinking how I should love other colors more. My wardrobe is overflowing with pink accessories. I enjoy fashion magazines and pretty pictures of women and apparel and the notion of looking really good. I love bedazzling. I love shimmery makeup. I work out like a madwoman so I can make myself look acceptable in pants that are coated with black leather. There’s such joy in caring about my appearance. I enjoy dresses, and I wear them daily. Nothing makes me happier than my maxi dresses. I just can’t take maxi dresses seriously.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Reason: Excerpt 2 is easier to read because it is in the first person point of view. It makes more sense and flows smoother than the first excerpt,  which is written more abstractly. I think Excerpt 2 is better because you can imagine what the author looks like as you read it.

written_by_Ashni.Excerpt2: To be a feminist — perhaps, to be a woman at all — is to teeter on the edge of a chasm between principle and performance. This week I rode the subway for the first time in months. In a moment of hyperperception, I swept my awareness over the scene: dusty bottles at the edge of the track, a lone rat scurrying into the bowels of the public transit system, three men hulking at one side of a gum-stained bench, blasting Drake on a tinny speaker. I found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception. Was I to admonish these men for listening to an artist well-known for wrapping misogyny in a catchy tune and feeding it to vulnerable audiences of young, troubled men? Did they expect this of me —were they waiting for my reprimand, already preparing their rebuttal? Should I be bracing myself for a flurry of calm downs and lighten ups? I did none of these things. Instead I found myself nodding slightly to the beat. Because, to tell the truth — it was a catchy tune. Perhaps this makes me a bad feminist. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for wearing pink flowy maxi dresses that highlight my femininity, a choice in line with the beauty standards and fashion requirements long used to subjugate women — to make women seem weaker, more delicate, more frivolous. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for ceding, at times, to this perception of the feminine as frail and foolish when it conveniences me: allowing a gallant male stranger to change my tire on the side of the road or letting my professional persona slip in a rare moment of vulnerability. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for thinking any of this at all — by discounting my true nature, I am participating in the classic erasure of women’s personal desires in favor of the welfare of others. Perhaps I am a bad feminist. But I am also a tired feminist. Where does it end? Am I to be trapped forever in this infinite moral calculation of every action and every thought? Candidly, I don’t mind being a bad feminist, if it means I can be like the subway rat — revolting and dirty, maybe, but free to scurry at my whim.

As far as effectiveness though, again I felt that excerpt 1 was more effective for me since it spoke the way I would.  Overall however, since we are looking for writing quality, I did feel that the writing quality of excerpt 2 was superior since it did give more explanation of things and was perhaps more stylized.

In a moment of hyperperception, I swept my awareness over the scene: dusty bottles at the edge of the track, a lone rat scurrying into the bowels of the public transit system, three men hulking at one side of a gum-stained bench, blasting Drake on a tinny speaker. I found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception. Was I to admonish these men for listening to an artist well-known for wrapping misogyny in a catchy tune and feeding it to vulnerable audiences of young, troubled men? Did they expect this of me —were they waiting for my reprimand, already preparing their rebuttal? Should I be bracing myself for a flurry of calm downs and lighten ups? I did none of these things. Instead I found myself nodding slightly to the beat. Because, to tell the truth — it was a catchy tune. Perhaps this makes me a bad feminist. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for wearing pink flowy maxi dresses that highlight my femininity, a choice in line with the beauty standards and fashion requirements long used to subjugate women — to make women seem weaker, more delicate, more frivolous. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for ceding, at times, to this perception of the feminine as frail and foolish when it conveniences me: allowing a gallant male stranger to change my tire on the side of the road or letting my professional persona slip in a rare moment of vulnerability. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for thinking any of this at all — by discounting my true nature, I am participating in the classic erasure of women’s personal desires in favor of the welfare of others. Perhaps I am a bad feminist. But I am also a tired feminist. Where does it end? Am I to be trapped forever in this infinite moral calculation of every action and every thought? Candidly, I don’t mind being a bad feminist, if it means I can be like the subway rat — revolting and dirty, maybe, but free to scurry at my whim.
written_by_Ashni.Excerpt2: I have a confession to make: I am a feminist, and I’m pretty bad at it. When I drive to work, I listen to thuggish rap at a very loud volume even though the lyrics are degrading to women, and this habit is a not-so-occasional source of shame. I am a feminist, and I enjoy fashion magazines. I watch The Bachelor and romantic comedies, and I’ve shrieked during the Fifty Shades of Grey trailer. I have incredible vocabulary skills, but sometimes I speak as though I am a delicate flower untouched by the grit of profanity. I will never ever know what to do with my hair. I think women are beautiful, interesting objects, which can be the start of a problem but also possibly the solution. I care what people think. I am a boss, and I am sometimes inappropriately affectionate with my employees. I am a doormat with people I love. I am polite and accommodating with customers in the store beneath my apartment even though they complain about me living above their precious store. I want to be in charge and respected and in control, but I want to be taken care of and have my hand held when I am unsure. I want to be strong and professional, but I resent being called a strong female character, because that phrase suggests there is an original archetype, and then secondary archetypes of women—everything but strong. I hate politics, and I don’t want to have to make political choices. Politicians scare the shit out of me, because they talk like salesmen, and I’m a sucker for a good salesman and a smooth line. I also live-tweet the Smithsonians and assorted other CW television shows. Pink is my favorite color, and I get hives just thinking how I should love other colors more. My wardrobe is overflowing with pink accessories. I enjoy fashion magazines and pretty pictures of women and apparel and the notion of looking really good. I love bedazzling. I love shimmery makeup. I work out like a madwoman so I can make myself look acceptable in pants that are coated with black leather. There’s such joy in caring about my appearance. I enjoy dresses, and I wear them daily. Nothing makes me happier than my maxi dresses. I just can’t take maxi dresses seriously.
written_by_Ashni.Reason:
I like excerpt 2 better for it's repetition and the reinforcement of the who the character is through the repeating sentences of 'I am' and the first person nature of the writing. it also has an element of humour with references to 'thuggish rap' and 'Fifty Shades of Grey'.

Excerpt 1 seems so much more confused and the repetition in this sentence is unnecessary and confusing, it disrupts the fluency of the excerpt  'found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception'.

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: I often long to be a better feminist. I know what a good feminist, a correct feminist, looks like. A woman who shouts down men who try to dominate her, a woman who refuses to ever be under the thumb of a man and shows up at all the right marches and always has her pink pussy hat at the ready for whatever protests comes next. I see those women, and I respect them, and often, I want to be them. But the fact of the matter is sometimes when men try to dominate me I let them, so they can mow my lawn without much of a fuss. When my father rattles off five misogynistic things in a row on our phone call I am silent, because I am too tired to fight back. And sometimes it is too cold outside to protest, pink pussy hat or no pink pussy hat. I want to be a good feminist, one that believes that women can do anything by themselves and we don't need any man. But sometimes I long to be cared for, sometimes I think I really do need a man. I long to be soft and weepy, and wear long flowing dresses and lipstick. This is the type of women the patriarchy praises, and feminists despise - and sometimes that is the type of woman I want to be. I want to be a good feminist, but often I am a bad feminist. I like dancing to rap songs with lyrics that are categorically misogynistic. I like wearing pink and scrolling through Pinterest pictures of those 'perfect' women that I know are there to make all us regular women feel terrible about ourselves. I like wearing those long maxi dresses that make me look like I could be on a farm, tending chickens and popping out babies dutifully for my husband. Not only do I like wearing those dresses, but I even have opinions on those dresses -- there are certain prints I love and other prints I find gauche, and when I see women wearing the latter I judge them. Another thing a good feminist would never do. And yet - I believe in the equality of the sexes. I am against male domination. I love women, and I want women to thrive. I just refuse to step up onto the pedestal of 'good feminist'. If I did, I'd fall. I'm a bad feminist.

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: I breathed in the night air that might or might not have smelled like blossoms. Looking at the incomparable skyline of Manhattan, I felt a familiar thrill - one I'd never been able to explain, though I knew it came from seeing those tiny illuminated windows set against the massive forms that contained them.The thrill was so intense and singular that it must have been more than just the visual relationship, for apart from a cityscape, nothing natural or man-made held my attention long enough to provoke it. What I saw, I thought, was a material form of the second person plural, the true subject of art. It was sublime, a plural subject, skyline as collective body coming into being, a body that didn't exist yet, something to which you could belong in the future and sometimes in the present tense. It only appeared solid, towering, but all the things that produced the sublime effects were bad: titanic banks bundling debt against the general welfare, measurable traces of antidepressants in the water supply, traffic networks poisoning the air, and ever-worsening storms. I'd long felt that one wanted to be an artist to make bad forms of collectivity appear as the promise of an almost unimaginable good: not reified abstraction, poorly disguised negation of the one in the many, but the emerging collective that would do justice to the wrongs absorbed by the bodies below the skyline. Tonight the fiction of the world—all my strongest perceptions, including rare fictions of participation in a benevolent collectivity—had gathered around Noor as if she were a black hole. Through her I was being changed more fully into a thing, a person among persons, and the experience was only horrible to the extent that it wasn't total. The uncanny feeling of not being identical with yourself, of being a stranger to your own experience, is profoundly alienating, yet it holds a glimmer of utopian hope. This sense of dislocation is available to be felt as a rearticulation, a promise that the past can be unlocked in the present. written_by_Sara.Excerpt2: The scent of blossoms colors the night, and New York in its entirety fits very neatly and completely into my hands. For instance, between my thumb and my index, lights flicker on and off in a miniature window. If I elongate my fingers I could also hold the silver skyscrapers tearing into the clouds. How astonishing; the skyline’s ants and beasts fit right, and wrong, into my palms. Back in my father's village nothing, absolutely nothing, fit into my hands. There were no neat edges anywhere, no contrast, nothing for me to want to try to hold. In short, there is no place I feel less alone than here, alone on this bench in New York, where the skyline is ours, and we are the skyline, my eyes staring straight into the material manifestation of a second person plural. In the future, they will say this skyline was synonymous with every art, every intimate form that has ever, or will ever, exist. To say we are the skyline is to confirm a collective identity, to confirm a stake in what makes up the city's sublime marrow; bundled debt, traces of antidepressants in the water, traffic networks, and shifting weather patterns. As an artist it will be my mission to transmute bad forms of collectivity into a sculpture of the communal body of the future. There is something Noor said once, in response to my ideas about the fiction of the world, that I am desperately trying to forget. We were not speaking the way people speak, necessarily, but more like skies, or skylines, when a passing cloud whispered something about a mirror. The disembodied voice said one cannot recognize oneself and at once be identical with oneself. But one plus one plus one equals three, if my math is correct. So maybe we multiply, keep multiplying, and our past and present and future selves never leave, and maybe that is what Noor really meant when she said the world has no genre you can name. The midnight air does nothing to unflatten my hair beneath the bandana. I would mistake this moment for a dream if I had not just consumed an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice all over my fingers. I vaguely remember a dream of myself as an old man, maybe an old woman, my fingers free of both tiny windows and the stain of fruit, and with this memory of the future I experience a mild lacrimal event, and I feel very alone, and very together.

The narrative of the character's thoughts flow logically from their thoughts to the idea Noor had, without explicitly introducing her, the reader can understand that they are talking about another person which is much more difficult to realise in Excerpt 1 due to the complexity of the sentence structures.

written_by_Hank.Excerpt1: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?

written_by_Hank.Excerpt1: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?
written_by_Hank.Excerpt2: I breathed in the night air that might or might not have smelled like blossoms. Looking at the incomparable skyline of Manhattan, I felt a familiar thrill - one I'd never been able to explain, though I knew it came from seeing those tiny illuminated windows set against the massive forms that contained them.The thrill was so intense and singular that it must have been more than just the visual relationship, for apart from a cityscape, nothing natural or man-made held my attention long enough to provoke it. What I saw, I thought, was a material form of the second person plural, the true subject of art. It was sublime, a plural subject, skyline as collective body coming into being, a body that didn't exist yet, something to which you could belong in the future and sometimes in the present tense. It only appeared solid, towering, but all the things that produced the sublime effects were bad: titanic banks bundling debt against the general welfare, measurable traces of antidepressants in the water supply, traffic networks poisoning the air, and ever-worsening storms. I'd long felt that one wanted to be an artist to make bad forms of collectivity appear as the promise of an almost unimaginable good: not reified abstraction, poorly disguised negation of the one in the many, but the emerging collective that would do justice to the wrongs absorbed by the bodies below the skyline. Tonight the fiction of the world—all my strongest perceptions, including rare fictions of participation in a benevolent collectivity—had gathered around Noor as if she were a black hole. Through her I was being changed more fully into a thing, a person among persons, and the experience was only horrible to the extent that it wasn't total. The uncanny feeling of not being identical with yourself, of being a stranger to your own experience, is profoundly alienating, yet it holds a glimmer of utopian hope. This sense of dislocation is available to be felt as a rearticulation, a promise that the past can be unlocked in the present. It is the paradoxical hope that in the moment you realize you are not yourself, you experience the possibility of becoming another, allowing the past to be reconfigured, rewritten in the now.I thought all this at midnight on a cheap folding bench with my hair flattened by a bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, tearing up a little—a mild lacrimal event—projecting myself into this scene from the future.

written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt1: Of course I didn’t think of it as cooking. In my mind it was just boiling spaghetti. I’d pull on my windbreaker and canvas sneakers, hop on my old bike and pedal to the neighborhood specialty store and gather the tools and ingredients I’d need to make spaghetti. A big pot, a thousand-yen strainer, two plates, a kitchen timer, a quart of olive oil, a head of garlic, and two onions. Supermarkets that catered to foreigners sold spaghetti. Displayed on their shelves were about ten brands in packages of every imaginable color. I bought a different brand and a small tin of spices each week. The old wooden creel hung from the handlebar would rattle and groan under the load on the way home. It just so happened that I had an old roasted-coffee mill in the cabinet under the sink that I could adjust to make minced garlic. Then I filled the place with the tantalizing aroma of garlic, onion, and olive oil, and I’d cook spaghetti sauce by the gallon and bend my head over each day’s spaghetti. Alone, at the kitchen table, no TV, no radio. Spaghetti was the only thing I could think of that was perfect for a meal eaten alone. Each and every time I’d prepare one extra little salad and one extra pot of tea…and each and every time my spaghetti would be submerged, swallowed up. Completely. So it was Spaghetti Days, from Sunday to Sunday.
written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt2: I call them the Spaghetti Days (they lasted an entire week but the singular week standing alone bothers me). On my way home from work, I’d pass the kitchen utility store where, in the shop window, there sat a stack of metal pots. I wanted the bottom one, the one shining against the rain the day I stepped through the shop door. Buying an empty pot felt wrong—too spacious—so I also bought an egg timer. But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. And being alone, there were always leftovers I’d scoop into a plastic container. At the end of the week, when it couldn’t fit any more spaghetti, I emptied all of it into the trash. No matter how hard I scrubbed the container, I couldn’t get the red stains out. I threw out the container too.
written_by_Benjamin.Reason: Excerpt 1 is more effective - it grabs you immediately because the first sentence is intriguing and you're not entirely sure where it's going. The language is evocative and descriptive. Both are fluent but again excerpt 1 has more flair to it. The ideas flow well but it's more than that, it's actually interesting to read.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: During that time I was much consumed by spaghetti. The process of cooking it was satisfying, but the idea of perfecting it was addictive. Like any dedicated student, I gathered the necessary equipment. I purchased a large pot and a kitchen timer from the specialty store across town and stocked up on spices, tomatoes, and all the pastas under the sun. The supermarket I bought the ingredients from was a place that catered to foreigners, but no one seemed to question my presence there. In a way, spaghetti and I were still strangers to each other. Back in my apartment, the experimenting began. What I lacked in formal training I had to make up for in creativity. I cooked feverishly. The smell of garlic was in my hair; the smell of onion was in the carpet; the smell of olive oil was in the wallpaper. Spaghetti sauce consumed me and the place I called home. It even spilled into my dreams. It was very important that I only ate spaghetti alone. It’s the kind of dish that insists on solitude. Before I knew it, I was following a new routine. Spaghetti was the centerpiece of every meal—balanced out, of course, by tea and a simple salad. My blissful Spaghetti Days stretched on and on from Sunday to Sunday. If there was an end in sight, I didn’t want to see it.

I purchased a large pot and a kitchen timer from the specialty store across town and stocked up on spices, tomatoes, and all the pastas under the sun. The supermarket I bought the ingredients from was a place that catered to foreigners, but no one seemed to question my presence there. In a way, spaghetti and I were still strangers to each other. Back in my apartment, the experimenting began. What I lacked in formal training I had to make up for in creativity. I cooked feverishly. The smell of garlic was in my hair; the smell of onion was in the carpet; the smell of olive oil was in the wallpaper. Spaghetti sauce consumed me and the place I called home. It even spilled into my dreams. It was very important that I only ate spaghetti alone. It’s the kind of dish that insists on solitude. Before I knew it, I was following a new routine. Spaghetti was the centerpiece of every meal—balanced out, of course, by tea and a simple salad. My blissful Spaghetti Days stretched on and on from Sunday to Sunday. If there was an end in sight, I didn’t want to see it.
written_by_Sophia.Reason: This passage builds gradually like a movie with each detail leading naturally to the next. Wooden creel and boiling spaghetti makes the passage feels more real than abstract. The use of descriptive phrases like one extra salad and one extra pot of tea"" draws a more vivid emotional picture of loneliness without having to give so much details.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: Of course I didn’t think of it as cooking. In my mind it was just boiling spaghetti. A big pot, a thousand-yen strainer, two plates, a kitchen timer, a quart of olive oil, a head of garlic, and two onions. Supermarkets that catered to foreigners sold spaghetti. Displayed on their shelves were about ten brands in packages of every imaginable color. I bought a different brand and a small tin of spices each week. The old wooden creel hung from the handlebar would rattle and groan under the load on the way home. It just so happened that I had an old roasted-coffee mill in the cabinet under the sink that I could adjust to make minced garlic. Then I filled the place with the tantalizing aroma of garlic, onion, and olive oil, and I’d cook spaghetti sauce by the gallon and bend my head over each day’s spaghetti. Alone, at the kitchen table, no TV, no radio. Spaghetti was the only thing I could think of that was perfect for a meal eaten alone. Each and every time I’d prepare one extra little salad and one extra pot of tea…and each and every time my spaghetti would be submerged, swallowed up. Completely. So it was Spaghetti Days, from Sunday to Sunday.

written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: Around seven years ago now I would go down to the Italian Market, weekends, to stock up on what I soon deemed the essentials: oregano, bay leaves, fennel seeds, butter, lemon. Among others. Nothing in my life pointed to this beginning. No crises or wayward desires, no history of culinary skills resurfaced, and I cannot say, exactly, what became of me during this time. Why I found myself in the aisles of specialty stores, several miles from home. Why I, each weekend, sought a furtherance: going beyond what I had cooked the week prior, with more tools, sauces, and research on what breed of spaghetti I would cook next. I tracked down a Le Creuset stockpot, a pasta roller, an egg timer. I spent too many hours over my stove at home, simmering garlic in olive oil, and over the cutting board on my countertop, chopping onions, tomatoes, basil. Though innocent at first, soon this meal prep encompassed every evening, Sunday through Sunday, and in this way I practiced what I now call my Spaghetti Days. During this time I never shared a meal with anyone else, coming to believe that spaghetti, along with my evening earl gray and caesar salad, was best enjoyed alone. Soon I realized it wasn’t desire that brought me to the habit, but ritualistic necessity. It was about hands, and what it meant to keep them moving. As soon as this realization came, all the magic of preparing spaghetti washed away.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: I'm rounding off this untidy decade, meeting my deadline, and choosing to let my lovers live and unite them at the end. I want to give Robbie and Cecilia what they lost out on in life. They both died because of a simple mistake which, although it grew in significance over the years, was not difficult to expunge. Or rather, I've always known the choice was mine. Was it right, however, to let them forgive? I've no doubt my fellow criminals are either behind bars or in important salaried positions. Hypocrites—I needed their praise and confirmation, and my sisters' doubts and contempt, in order to be cured. But now I must sleep. I will close my eyes and sleep. What purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on June 1, 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station? What sense or hope or satisfaction could a reader draw from such an account? Who would want to believe that they never met again, never fulfilled their love? Who would want to believe that, except in the service of the bleakest realism? And what of that monstrous sister who systematically destroyed the love of her own sibling? I couldn't do it to them.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: I am Briony, and I am sad to report on the tragic fate of two lovers, Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis. Because I invented them myself, their tragedy is my own fault, but because their characters are based in reality, I cannot help but feel loyal to the truth. The fact is that Robbie and Cecilia died during World War II. Robbie succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes, and Cecilia perished in a bombing at Balham Underground station. Neither of them knew that I had committed a terrible wrong against them both. In my youth, I was wickedly jealous of Robbie and Cecilia and resented the affection they held for one another. Not because I desired either of them, but because I was angry and lonely and hiding in a bunker of cynicism. I was a postboy, and when Robbie went off to war, I would intercept the letters he sent to Cecelia and slide them into the rain-filled gutters. I did the same to Cecelia’s letters, and their correspondence slowly dwindled. Eventually, they stopped writing to each other altogether. I’ve been approaching this all wrong. Now is the time to let Robbie and Cecelia survive and be together, even if only in these pages. Telling the truth wouldn’t do any good, because it’s an ugly truth. I never saw Robbie and Cecelia again, their love stayed unfulfilled, and their few remaining letters are preserved only in a war museum. Maybe truth is not always better than mercy. Maybe hope survives through lies.
written_by_Sophia.Reason: I really enjoy the rhetorical questions in excerpt 1 as they are gripping and intriguing. This is a really effective technique. The varying sentence lengths also keep you interested as it varies the pace. As with all these examples they are both coherent and fluent, but excerpt 1 seems to be more effective overall.
