written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: The truth is much uglier than the sweet story I’ve given them. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis never saw each other again, both having perished during the war. Robbie fell to septicemia at Bray Dunes, his wounds never healing right. Cecilia, my glamorous older sister, died in a bombing at the Balham Underground, dressed in the same rationed rags as any other woman. They died alone, a fault I must now agonizingly take the blame for. It was my callous childishness that ripped Robbie from Cecilia, but it is my better nature that has prompted me to write them a better ending. They find each other again, they live, and they are happy. What good would it do, I beg to know, in telling the foul truth? I’ll tell it, here and now, if only to prove my point. I never saw either of them again that year, how could I, after what I had done to Cecilia? Their love died with them, isolated and unfulfilled, with the sole evidence that they knew each other being those romantic letters preserved only in a war museum. I cannot imagine truth is worth more than the merciful fiction, but I struggle even now to know for certain if my rewrite of history is fair. I’d like to think that this hopeful conclusion, regardless of how factual it may be, holds greater value than an honest, but tragic account.

written_by_Devin.Excerpt1: I’d spoken with Reva last week, but it was a short conversation filled mostly with platitudes. She’d seemed distracted and said she was at the gym. When the news broke about the towers, I called her a few times, but she didn’t pick up. Without thinking, I went immediately to the store to purchase a TV/VCR machine. Suddenly the most important thing was to record all the news footage that was blaring at me from out of my TV. I thought briefly about calling Trevor, then remembered that he was in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably sipping a drink with some spiky, inedible part of a fruit in it, completely unaware of what had happened. Once the sun went down and I still hadn’t heard from her, I realized that Reva was lost, likely for good. For days I sat watching and rewatching the footage I’d taped of the attacks, unable to move from in front of the TV save to piss or search the bathroom cabinet for more pills. There was a video of a woman leaping from the North Tower, and though it was too grainy for me to ever be able to tell if it was Reva, I liked imagining that it was.She wore a grey pencil skirt with black tights and stilettos – one still gripping her foot while the other had torn free, suspended in the air. She looked so beautiful, jumping like that into the unknown, that I took a kind of strange and holy comfort in her courage.
written_by_Devin.Excerpt2: "You should hang out more," I told Reva. "You'd like that, huh?" I could hear the whir of the machines in the background. "I gotta go, weirdo. I'm at the gym."On the morning of September 11, 2001, I went straight from the bodega where I got my coffee to Circuit City and charged a new TV/VCR combo on my Visa to record the news coverage. Trevor was on his honeymoon in Barbados. Everything was happening as it was supposed to. Reva was now "lost." For a full week I watched the same footage of the planes hitting the Twin Towers, the burning people plummeting, the buildings crumbling at the end like collapsing sand castles from every angle the news had to show.One woman leapt from a window from the North Tower and somehow caught my attention. She had on a skirt or a dress and was barefoot. As she spun, her stockings caught the updraft like sails, and I could see the outline of her thighs. She fell so gracefully. It looked almost like she was dancing. If I squinted, she looked like Reva. Of course I loved her—I had spent the last year mourning her as though she were dead. But I didn't cry. I wasn't hurt. I didn't feel sad. I just admired her, looked up at her there, so far above me and so elegant.

written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: The last time I spoke to Reva, she was distant. Eager to get back to sweating on the elliptical, or stair-master, or whatever absurd machine she was convinced would keep away the horrors of arm flab. She’s distant now, too, but in a new way. That day, Trevor was on his honeymoon in Barbados, but Reva felt farther. She was gone, lost. I still feel a faint throb of theft when I think of them. On the morning of September 11th , I bought a TV/VCR and recorded the towers going down. When I find myself drifting, floating back to the state I had been in that previous year, I turn on the recording and watch. The footage isn’t soothing, it’s scalding—it wakes me up and keeps me conscious. In one clip, my favorite clip, a woman leaps from a window ledge in the North Tower. She looks enough like Reva that if I were feeling sentimental, I could pretend it’s her. The edge of her pencil skirt whipping up could be Reva’s knock-off designer, her shoes flying from her feet and floating up past her head could be Reva’s second hand Manolos, the glints of sunlight that could be Reva’s grandmother’s ring. But it doesn’t have to be. I don’t need her to be Reva. In dreams, when you feel like you’re falling, you jolt awake. I need her to wake me up.

written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: A billionaire once invited me to lunch at his club in London. It was a grand place, but the billionaire wore skinny jeans, a hooded top, and designer trainers without a care in the world. He was very keen to show me his latest software project, which was a program that could predict which employees in a company would next betray their boss. I had to catch a plane immediately afterwards and so was a little restless, and he insisted on paying for my taxi to the airport, which was nice, since I'd come with a suitcase. We were supposed to be talking about a literary magazine he wanted to start, and I hadn't expected his personal security software to come up. But when we sat down and started, it was he who told me the story of his life. I assembled the biography: a humble beginning, the lessons in work and intellect, and finally this  tawny-haired and surprisingly well-muscled figure at the table across from me. I guess he imagined that the literary magazine might provide some sort of entrée into the practice of writing, seeing as he'd got and done pretty much everything else with his money. He told me a lot more – about the complexity and immensity of his entrepreneurial schemes, such as a floating wind farm that would house and provide credit for its workers and thereby solve the problem of world poverty and ecocide; or another scheme he had for legally disposing of lawyers from people's personal lives. He also mentioned that he'd taken up playing drums in a rock band every Thursday night, because why not; and that he was presently expecting his eleventh child, counting the Guatemalan quadruplets he and his wife had adopted earlier. The billionaire talked for so long that I couldn’t keep up with it all, I was almost too exhausted to follow. Waitresses kept arriving, removing dishes and bringing huge plates of lobster and bottles of fine wine. His focus was so scattered, his enthusiasm so limitless, it was almost like that of a child. Enjoy yourself in Athens, he said, putting me in the taxi afterwards, though I didn't remember mentioning I was going there.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: I was invited to lunch by a billionaire who wanted to start a literary magazine. The London club was opulent, the atmosphere carefully crafted through gilded light fixtures and dark accents. I was late, carrying my heavy suitcase and sweating, but the billionaire wore casual clothes and seemed unbothered by my lateness, launching into an explanation of his software project for predicting employee betrayal. The literary journal had not come up when the waitress brought bread to us, nor when she brought a range of appetizers. I realized the billionaire had ordered for us both. He insisted then on paying for a taxi to the airport, a generosity I would not decline given the rush of my morning. As we ate, he unfurled his life story. ‘It’s all what you’d expect,’ he said. ‘Rags-to-riches, you know—to be rich and unbothered, that’s the real achievement. To feel calm,’ he told me. ‘That’s what it allows.’ I wondered if he thought of the literary magazine as an entry point into writing. Everyone wants to write, I’ve noticed; everyone imagines themselves a writer, even if they have never put pen to paper. The billionaire had funded a good many ambitious ventures. A floating wind farm with worker houses, and something about a scheme to eliminate lawyers for managing personal matters. The waitress brought small plates, caviar and shaved truffle and mint suspended artfully over a scallop. The billionaire played drums in a rock band to relax. He was expecting his eleventh child, a number of children he knew and hoped that I would balk at, and explained that four of his children were adopted Guatemalan quadruplets. The waitress came along with another round of drinks. A perfect cube of ice sat in the center of each. I was struggling to process most of what the billionaire had said, the dishes before us becoming more and more luxurious, and expensive. His frenetic, scattered storytelling and sweet enthusiasm felt childlike against the opulence of our experience, of this lunch. When he put me in my taxi, he said ‘Enjoy yourself in Athens.’ This surprised me, as I didn’t recall telling him my destination. Actually I could not remember saying anything during our lunch.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Reason: I do not like the voice of author in excerpt one as right from the start it feels braggadocios without even fully knowing what the point to the story is. Excerpt 2 is much cleaner and laid out in a way that feels interesting and lends itself to my curiosity.

written_by_Caroline_Porter.Excerpt1: The billionaire had invited me to lunch with him at a London club. When I arrived, I was surprised by how casually he dressed, in jeans and a white button-down. He told me about the rock band he played drums in, and that he was expecting his eleventh child soon. This was in addition to the four Guatemalan quadruplets he had already adopted. It felt like too many children to me. I wondered if perhaps he thought that by creating this magazine, he might also fashion himself as a writer capable of being published in it. The idea seemed a stretch to me, but perhaps the billionaire was used to spanning such extreme logical leaps. The leap from man to billionaire was certainly larger than billionaire to writer. I was struggling to follow my own line of thinking. The waitress kept appearing, bringing brightly colored drinks and dishes that alternated between tasting too rich and too pungent. It had the opposite effect on the billionaire. Amidst the bright colors and flavors, the billionaire's face shone like a young boy who had been suddenly surrounded by mountains of his favorite sweets. When the food and drink had finally been swept away and the bill paid, he put me and my heavy suitcase in the taxi. Enjoy yourself in Athens, he said, which was a surprise. I hadn't recalled ever mentioning my destination.

written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: "Race doesn't really exist for you because it has never been a barrier. Black folks don't have that choice. Like, growing up in Nigeria, I knew I was black, but I didn't really think about it until I came to America. Then I came here and—God, it hits you immediately. Race becomes everything. You can't say in good faith race doesn't matter when you are dating a white man. The minute you step outside, things are apparent. When somebody walks into a bar that you are sitting in with your white husband, they don't see a man and a woman; they see a white man and a black woman. It doesn't matter what they say. At the grocery store, they'll ask you, separately, if you need help, because, of course, it's such a stretch to imagine that you're together. And you are thinking about that, you are aware of that, but your white partner is not thinking about it in the same way. Or he is not thinking about it at all.So you stifle your feelings because you don't want him to dismiss you by saying you're being paranoid, or remind you that, hey, until the sixties, you all wouldn't even have been able to date, so at least you're doing good. And of course if you say any of this to your nice liberal American friends, they say, 'But we're not like that.' You see, in America's public discourse, 'but' is usually a prelude to rationalization. And when you say, 'but we're not like that' to black people, what you're also saying is that you're refusing to acknowledge the truth of their experience."The host, a Frenchwoman who lived with her American husband, looked amused, as though enjoying the possibility that discord was coming.The poet appeared uncomfortable, eager to suggest a safer topic. "Darling, should I save the onion dip?" she asked the host.The other guests were all watching as though they had never imagined they would feel this way: enjoined in intellectual discomfort by a person they had thought was intellectually like them. Ifemelu was emboldened by the white wine. A part of her wanted to apologize for not playing to the right audience, but a part of her knew she would do it all again.Perhaps she had gone too far, but she was plugged in now, the center of their attention. Even Blaine's expression was unreadable; she could not tell what he was thinking. She took another sip of wine. "So, my ex-boyfriend Curt was the first white man I dated."
written_by_Cara.Excerpt2: Ifemelu took another sip of her chardonnay. She knew she should let the subject drop, but the wine was giving her a slight buzz that made her feel emboldened, and she suddenly felt they all needed to hear what she had to say. "Racism is nowhere near over in America," she said, "despite what we may tell our white friends and lovers because we don't want to make them feel uncomfortable." She gestured with her wine glass, pointing at her hosts, then at herself. "The truth is, I've never been more aware that I'm Black than I have been since coming to America. In Nigeria, I hardly thought of my race. But here, I'm constantly reminded of it, and not just by racists and rednecks like you might think, but by white liberals, academics, even other Black people, to tell you the truth. And to make matters worse, I can't say anything about it, or I'll be seen as making a fuss since we've apparently come so far. They'll point out that I have a white boyfriend and no one gives me any trouble for it, when interracial marriage used to be illegal. They call that progress when that's the bare minimum. Frankly, it's patronizing." Ifemelu looked pointedly at the poet, who had kept her head down and was picking at her salad. The poet avoided her eye contact and instead turned to the hostess, as if she sensed an opportunity to change the subject. "This salad is so delicious," she said, holding up a forkful of greens. The hostess thanked her, but she was still watching Ifemelu with anticipation and maybe some detached amusement, since this wasn't her home country, and Ifemelu had said nothing about France. Her American husband, meanwhile, seemed excited to have his cadre of polite and well-educated liberals challenged by this unfamiliar woman, his friend's new girlfriend. Ifemelu reached for the wine glass again and looked up at Blaine to see if she'd gone too far, but his gaze was inscrutable, though fixed on her. Well, if what he loved about me is my mind, he can't be mad if I speak it, she thought. And if she said something too scandalous, she could always write them an apology note later. And before she could stop herself, she was telling them all the deeply personal stuff about her struggles while dating Curt.

written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: Ifemelu looks at her Frenchwoman host and her American husband, both grinning with rows of straight teeth, and puts down her wine glass. The wine loosens her tongue and she cannot help it when she says, "America is obsessed with race. I never realized how much until I moved here and now I can't get away from it." She speaks quickly, the words coming easily to her despite the many eyes now firmly fixed on her. With her captive audience, she could almost be a college professor, the kind that reminds her of cult leaders. The watching usually makes her skin crawl, but now it feels like the eyes are attached to ears that are earnestly listening. She tells them that every time she goes outside, she is acutely aware of her blackness in a way she has never experienced before. "Because I'm so aware," she says, "I'm extra-aware when I'm with a boyfriend. And it's not just me, it's everyone in an interracial relationship! You don't want your boyfriend accusing you of being too sensitive, you know? Men always call women crybabies, so you don't want him thinking you're any more emotional than he already believes. Confirmation bias! So you pretend it doesn't bother you, even though it really does. And you can't complain to anyone else about your white boyfriend, either, because there's always some old crone muttering about how, well," she pitches her voice for a biting mimicry. "Interracial relationships used to be illegal, which is so infantilizing to point out! Just because things used to be worse, doesn't mean I can't be frustrated by them still being bad!" she says, and she looks at her nice, liberal audience, and how they've all put down their forks as if eating would mean they aren't listening. They're leaning forward, watching her like a specimen under a microscope. Her hosts are chuckling to each other, but nodding along. Next to them, the poet, who has been a far quieter guest than Ifemelu, tugs at the Frenchwoman's sleeve to nervously compliment one of the side dishes. She absently thanks him and gestures for Ifemelu to keep going. Blaine's face is shuttered, and Ifemelu takes another sip of wine. Distantly, she thinks she might regret this tomorrow. She opens her mouth, though, and says, "It was like that with my ex-boyfriend, Curt." Blaine's lip twitches. Ifemelu says, "He just couldn't understand."

written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: Ifemelu looks at her Frenchwoman host and her American husband, both grinning with rows of straight teeth, and puts down her wine glass. The wine loosens her tongue and she cannot help it when she says, "America is obsessed with race. I never realized how much until I moved here and now I can't get away from it." She speaks quickly, the words coming easily to her despite the many eyes now firmly fixed on her. With her captive audience, she could almost be a college professor, the kind that reminds her of cult leaders. The watching usually makes her skin crawl, but now it feels like the eyes are attached to ears that are earnestly listening. She tells them that every time she goes outside, she is acutely aware of her blackness in a way she has never experienced before. "Because I'm so aware," she says, "I'm extra-aware when I'm with a boyfriend. And it's not just me, it's everyone in an interracial relationship! You don't want your boyfriend accusing you of being too sensitive, you know? Men always call women crybabies, so you don't want him thinking you're any more emotional than he already believes. Confirmation bias! So you pretend it doesn't bother you, even though it really does. And you can't complain to anyone else about your white boyfriend, either, because there's always some old crone muttering about how, well," she pitches her voice for a biting mimicry. "Interracial relationships used to be illegal, which is so infantilizing to point out! Just because things used to be worse, doesn't mean I can't be frustrated by them still being bad!" she says, and she looks at her nice, liberal audience, and how they've all put down their forks as if eating would mean they aren't listening. They're leaning forward, watching her like a specimen under a microscope. Her hosts are chuckling to each other, but nodding along. Next to them, the poet, who has been a far quieter guest than Ifemelu, tugs at the Frenchwoman's sleeve to nervously compliment one of the side dishes. She absently thanks him and gestures for Ifemelu to keep going. Blaine's face is shuttered, and Ifemelu takes another sip of wine. Distantly, she thinks she might regret this tomorrow. She opens her mouth, though, and says, "It was like that with my ex-boyfriend, Curt." Blaine's lip twitches. Ifemelu says, "He just couldn't understand."

When somebody walks into a bar that you are sitting in with your white husband, they don't see a man and a woman; they see a white man and a black woman. It doesn't matter what they say. At the grocery store, they'll ask you, separately, if you need help, because, of course, it's such a stretch to imagine that you're together. And you are thinking about that, you are aware of that, but your white partner is not thinking about it in the same way. Or he is not thinking about it at all.So you stifle your feelings because you don't want him to dismiss you by saying you're being paranoid, or remind you that, hey, until the sixties, you all wouldn't even have been able to date, so at least you're doing good. And of course if you say any of this to your nice liberal American friends, they say, 'But we're not like that.' You see, in America's public discourse, 'but' is usually a prelude to rationalization. written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: "It means something different, to be Black here. Something wide and heavy, and I wasn't expecting that, when I moved. You can meet someone, and they can seem perfect for you. But if they're white - when you go outside, that's all anyone cares about. Their whiteness, your Blackness. And you have to dodge the dirty looks people give you on the street. And if you want to talk about that, with your partner - suddenly you're the bad guy. You can't bring up how racism makes you feel because all of a sudden they're defensive and angry, they think you're calling them a racist. And they can't understand, really, what it feels like to be looked at the way people sometimes look at me. Like I'm nothing, or less than nothing." As Ifemelu spoke, Blaine's lips were pressing into a thin, straight line. He looked studiously at his fork, refusing to meet her eyes. A part of her brain cautioned her to stop talking, but the wine had made her tongue heavy and her jaw loose. "People are always saying to me - fifty years ago, you would have been locked up if you tried to date a white man, look at how far this country has come! That's all people ever want to talk about, how much progress has been made. Everyone expects me to be so grateful and happy to be here, but all I can think about is how awful it feels sometimes, to live here and always be thinking about how other people are seeing me." Ifemelu paused. Her own words were echoing in her ears, and she felt the stinging truth of them. The poet seized upon this break and pointed down at his plate. "How did you make these Brussels sprouts?" he said, and the French host seemed not to hear him at all; her eyes were trained on Ifemelu. "But why so pessimistic?" she asked, almost breathlessly, leaning in like Ifemelu was delivering scandalous gossip. "Maybe the people in your past were just wrong for you in some way. Maybe they're skewing your perception." Ifemelu drained the rest of her glass and tightened her fingers around the stem. "The people in my past didn't skew my perception - they showed me the truth," Ifemelu said bitterly. "Let me tell you about this one man I used to date - his name was Curt."

written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: It was early winter already, and once it got dark the room was piteously cold. While there was still light, my mother got up and went into the kitchen. She filled the biggest rice bowl with water, then put it on the gas burner and waited for it to come to the boil. She snipped a length of white thread from the spool in her sewing box, and gently pressed a small pair of scissors into the steaming water. When the pain became so insupportable that she could no longer stand up, she lay down in the middle of the room. Labor began at around midnight. Trembling with fear, she used a scrap of white cloth to swaddle the newborn, as thin as a rat, and tied the thread around the barely pulsating umbilical cord. Then she severed it. She held the baby to her breast and murmured, Live, please live. Go on living and become my son. She continued to murmur to herself even as its barely open eyes closed for the final time. Go on. Keep going. After that, silence. The cold from the earthen floor invaded her back. Soaked into and through her flesh. Matching her lifeless child.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman—the kind who bore such immense pain that she gave birth to it, all alone at the onset of the longest winter on record. The biting cold was nothing but a faint chill compared to the icy fear whispering in her ears. Was she strong enough, capable enough, to do this? Even as she boiled water to sterilize the scissors she'd use for cutting the umbilical cord, she worried the answer was a resounding no. With shaking hands, she fashioned a gown from loose fabric she kept tucked away in her sewing box. As though the faux-hospital garb could imbue the experience with a semblance of professionalism. The kind that would ward off infant death. It didn't, of course.The baby lived for a precious few moments, wheezing as my mother prayed—mindless and desperate—to a deaf god that her child should live on. Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.My mother rocked the dead baby against her chest and felt the chill of the floor creep up into the soles of her feet, freezing her into a statue of grief. Mother and baby, alone; forever.
written_by_Rachael.Reason: The story flows along in time and the reader is taken along with it. The language is elaborate but simple to understand and again brings the reader close. The story flows well and the sentence where the baby dies is carefully crafted and powerful. In contrast excerpt  2 jumps about in time too much and it is difficult to read and understand.

written_by_Devanshi.Excerpt1: The early days of winter remind my mother of her dead child. My father knew that my mother was due at any moment, but the roads were icy and the entire landscape had turned bare and hostile, preventing him from returning home.My mother was in labor, all by herself at home, and the ripples of her screams were absorbed by the walls, making cracks that had not existed before. In the kitchen, she tried as best as she could. She kept some water to boil in a small pot to sterilize a pair of kitchen scissors. She took off her clothes and quickly fashioned a hospital gown from some fabric that was guarded in a sewing box.Gripped by fear and pain so intense that she felt larger and more forceful than the dazzle of winter outside, my mother held a baby—slippery and blood-covered—in her arms. She had pushed and pushed, and had severed the umbilical cord with the hot pair of scissors that had burned her fingers. She chanted an old prayer, a common plea for life, but felt the warmth of the baby's body fading.My mother tells me that is when she stopped screaming. In a fleeting moment, the alchemy of the house shifted: life became death. The coldness of the floor seeped through her own body. It became impossible to tell whether the air was so still because of the cold, or her grief, or both.

written_by_Devin.Excerpt2: My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong. It was early winter. The trees were bare and the ground hard. With shaky steps, she described pacing about the kitchen while she boiled water in order to sterilize the scissors that she knew she’d need to cut the cord. With the fabric in her sewing box, she fashioned a small gown and began to wear it. During the waves of pain from her contractions, she would grip at the kitchen counter hard. Eventually after hours of this the baby came out wet and covered in a fuzzy-looking substance. Still alone, she held the newborn. Chanting a desperate plea for the little thing’s survival over and over again. But after a fleeting moment of brilliant life, her newborn child went still and died. My mother lay on the floor of the kitchen. Silently, clutching at the lifeless body of what was once vibrant inside of her. As she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief, the warmth from her body departed into the frigid floor. As though the temperature of the house were somehow reflective of her inner state.
written_by_Devin.Reason: Excerpt one seemed better written than excerpt two, which did not flow as well. Both created an image of the birth and death of this woman's child but excerpt one did so while also relaying the emotion of that event. Excerpt two felt like it was just a description lacked the strength of that emotion.

When the pain became so insupportable that she could no longer stand up, she lay down in the middle of the room. Labor began at around midnight. Trembling with fear, she used a scrap of white cloth to swaddle the newborn, as thin as a rat, and tied the thread around the barely pulsating umbilical cord. Then she severed it. She held the baby to her breast and murmured, Live, please live. Go on living and become my son. She continued to murmur to herself even as its barely open eyes closed for the final time. Go on. Keep going. After that, silence. The cold from the earthen floor invaded her back. Soaked into and through her flesh. Matching her lifeless child.
written_by_Devin.Excerpt2: My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong. It was early winter. With the fabric in her sewing box, she fashioned a small gown and began to wear it. During the waves of pain from her contractions, she would grip at the kitchen counter hard. Eventually after hours of this the baby came out wet and covered in a fuzzy-looking substance. Still alone, she held the newborn. Chanting a desperate plea for the little thing’s survival over and over again. But after a fleeting moment of brilliant life, her newborn child went still and died. As she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief, the warmth from her body departed into the frigid floor. As though the temperature of the house were somehow reflective of her inner state.

written_by_Hank.Excerpt1: And so the day passed. In the center of the city, the maghrib rang out its ancient melody, warring with the Tamil music lilting out of the speakers of a passing rickshaw—the ocean swell of strings, the buoyant theme of an old Hollywood film. The aroma of filter coffee boiled up from the terraces of the cafes, which were filled with tourists from Tuscany, Madrid, Tyrol. In other neighborhoods, children rendezvoused with their peers in shady alleyways, holding tense diplomatic summits over their games of tag. The heat lingered over the city like a sinister spirit cavalry, a battalion of jinns casting spells over Elliot’s Beach; over the twin harbors and colonial promenade; over the government center and the inland districts; and back out again to one sea-green apartment building, on the fourth floor of which there were two empty verandahs. In the corresponding room, two men simultaneously awakened from their afternoon naps and stepped out onto these verandahs, which it should be said were no longer empty. Senior and Junior, as the men were called by their respective acquaintances, did not look at each other; nor did they watch the youth wander lazily from the streets to the promenade, passing marijuana cigarettes down the line like the world’s slowest relay team. Senior and Junior looked out at Elliot’s Beach, this strange sandy coin that had been cast away by fate.
written_by_Hank.Excerpt2: The day heated up and we heard the prayer bells in the temples, the bhangra beats from the music trucks plying their enthusiastic trade, the untuneful crying of children. It was time for coffee, and coffee, and coffee yet again, and lemon rice garnished with fried cashews, and all the other wondrous concoctions on offer in Madras. The two old men on the fourth floor of their sea-green building were released from their rooms by the day off like ships slipping their moorings, but they were rusty and they didn't go very far. Their names were blazoned across mailboxes and doorbells. Crowds of the young were descending upon Elliot's Beach, young men in cricket gear, young women deep in laughter and high fragrance, lovers hating their separation; and bikes, bikes, bikes. The sea was a water lily, the young people there were bees. Just a few short years ago Senior and Junior would have been down there too, scampering with the best, but now they had their own slow dance. They woke up just before noon and put on their two-day-old clothes. As if, by some mysterious machinery of fate, the timing wheels within their thickening, aging frames had been perfectly synchronized, they stepped out onto their verandahs at almost the same precise second and stood looking out into the world.
written_by_Hank.Reason: In the second excerpt,  the language used seem to be very simple and easy to understand a lot so as a result, I will definitely go for excerpt 2 in terms of simplicity, effectiveness and clarity. It makes the reading very simple and easy at the same time, ensuring there is accuracy.

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: One morning in a town quite near Chennai, the sun arose with a ferocity and began beating down on the town's residents, and there was no time to blink back dawn, the children were already awake and fussing for food, and Miss Aadhya had started on the first pot of coffee, and from her window she could hear Bollywood music, already blaring, and below her the old man whose name no one knew was praying, and above her, on the fourth floor of the Aquamarine building, Senior struggled against that veil that separates dream from reality, and broke through, and was awake. At the same time, his neighbor, Junior, awoke. The two men's eyes opened at the same time. Kabir was now calling to his friends, everyone making plans for an evening at the Elliot’s beach, the promise of cool water the only thing making it bearable to get through the hot afternoon. All the members of the town were connected to each other, as a marionette has strings attached to each of its joints, each small movement producing an equal and opposite reaction. Senior swung his legs out of bed and Junior finished brushing his teeth. The clamor of the town stirred something in both of them, and, with one elegant pull, they both lifted their heads and decided to go out, onto their own veranda.

written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: Under the heavy weight of the late afternoon sun, the city was bursting with heat, the sound of chanting prayers—Surya Mangalam, said for hope of peaceful evenings—sitar and tabla-heavy soundtracks, and children's cries rising like heat shimmers, with sweetened filter coffee laden in the air, one final push to get through to the fast-approaching dusk. Moving to an instinctual, silent rhythm, Senior and Junior rose as one, like two men bound by strings of fate, their walk to their verandahs as sure as the sun's journey across the sky until they sank into their chairs with the same achy movements, tilting their heads back once comfortable, two mirrors reflecting back at each other. Beneath them, a jubilant cheer rose up to greet the old men, and twin smiles stretched slowly across their faces, for they were soothed by their repetition and the companionship that repetition brings.

written_by_Yen.Excerpt1: My father wanted to take me to lunch. He found a restaurant unlike any I’d ever been to, unlike anything that existed in C. Any excitement I felt disappeared quickly. The waiter looked us up and down, seeing what we were immediately. I was pale from the winter, dressed in my worn, washed clothes. I wore spectacles, awkward and out of fashion, the kind you could buy at a steep discount. The waiter directed us to a shared table at the back of the restaurant, in front of the wash closet. At first my experience of discomfort was limited only to me. My father still had a big smile, ear to ear. But then I saw another father-daughter pair at a table in the restaurant’s big window. The girl was around my age, and pretty. She dealt with the restaurant staff confidently, with a confiding air, like they shared a special secret. I watched the girl longingly. Her tanned legs ended in delicate buckled shoes. I watched her eat food I could not identify. Back then, I’d never had yoghurt.As the waiter laughed and spoke to them in earshot of us, I saw my father growing red. “Those potatoes were pig slop,” he said after we left the restaurant, again and again. It embarrassed me. It was clear enough to both of us what had happened. At least, it was clear that we’d both had a bad time. I knew what he was saying. We had been treated as second-class citizens because we ordered the prix fixe, instead of selecting expensive dishes à la carte like the more sophisticated clientele. I wanted to forget about it. If we didn’t speak of the event, then perhaps it wasn’t real.
written_by_Yen.Excerpt2: The restaurant was an annex to the Trois-Couronnes.I had a pale face and was wearing my spectacles that day, which made me look sad. That wasn't the issue, though. My father and I had been seated at the table reserved for groups, on the far side of the dining room, and were ignored throughout the meal. At the next table, there was a man with his daughter, who was older than I was, maybe seventeen, sleek and tanned with short blonde hair. I remember a long, gilt-framed mirror hanging above their heads, reflecting endless repetitions of identical people. The girl talked confidently to her father and laughingly spooned up her yogurt. In those days, I didn't know what yogurt was. She seemed at home, oblivious to her surroundings, wearing no jacket or headscarf, simply her checkered summer dress. She made me feel awkward and ashamed, although I couldn't explain why, my only desire being to leave as soon as possible. Later on, walking along the streets, my father kept saying, "Those mashed potatoes looked like pig slop." For the first time, I realized that he had been marking time to continue, repeating the reason why he hadn't eaten anything on his plate. I didn't think of asking him what difference it made what the potatoes looked like. Deep down, he was upset at being treated as a second-class customer just because we weren't dining "à la carte" like the people sitting near us.
written_by_Yen.Reason: Excerpt 1 uses more simple English that is very comprehensible. "We had been treated as second-class citizens because we ordered the prix fixe, instead of selecting expensive dishes à la carte like the more sophisticated clientele".This line shows how well the ideas in the story flow together and how the narrator feels which in turn captures how the narrator felt due to class difference.

written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."

written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: The restaurant was an annex to the Trois-Couronnes.I had a pale face and was wearing my spectacles that day, which made me look sad. That wasn't the issue, though. My father and I had been seated at the table reserved for groups, on the far side of the dining room, and were ignored throughout the meal. At the next table, there was a man with his daughter, who was older than I was, maybe seventeen, sleek and tanned with short blonde hair. I remember a long, gilt-framed mirror hanging above their heads, reflecting endless repetitions of identical people. The girl talked confidently to her father and laughingly spooned up her yogurt. In those days, I didn't know what yogurt was. She seemed at home, oblivious to her surroundings, wearing no jacket or headscarf, simply her checkered summer dress. She made me feel awkward and ashamed, although I couldn't explain why, my only desire being to leave as soon as possible. Later on, walking along the streets, my father kept saying, "Those mashed potatoes looked like pig slop." For the first time, I realized that he had been marking time to continue, repeating the reason why he hadn't eaten anything on his plate. I didn't think of asking him what difference it made what the potatoes looked like. Deep down, he was upset at being treated as a second-class customer just because we weren't dining "à la carte" like the people sitting near us.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt2: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: "If I could tell my own father about this!" cried Samad. "One son, with his marmite on toast and his football games. The other, a downright fundamentalist! More Bengali than I ever was. What would he have done, my father, if he could see me now? He would have said, It serves you right, Samad. That is what you get for going somewhere you are only tolerated." Samad paused and took a long sip of his tea. "Oh, Irie," he continued. "If I’d known that England was the way that it is. A place where we are merely tolerated. A place where belonging and not belonging both feel like a trap. Was it not pure foolishness, then, to come here? Not sometimes, but every single day, I know it was a mistake. We should have stayed put. What didn’t we stay put?” Irie shook her head. “That is not true, surely, Samad,” she said. “It’s England. It’s what we have always wanted. We dreamed of this place all our lives." "We dreamed of a version of this place, certainly," said Samad. "Truthfully, I don’t know what I believe anymore. I thought I knew what it meant to be born somewhere. But now? What does it matter where you are born? How can you belong anywhere if you feel... adrift. Every day. Completely adrift."
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2:
"Well, life's dealt some rather unkind cards. One son, a pukka Englishman—a suit-wearing, diploma-carrying, Tory-voting coward—while my other son has gone from muttering one-liners about infidels to a bloody fundamentalist terrorist. I can't say it surprises me. Yes, I made a devil's pact; yes, yes—but please tell me where was the better option? My father, from whom I could never escape, made quite sure there was only one road to be taken. To hell with it. This is the suffering of the immigrant: of my generation and Archibald's, immigrants by necessity, English by residence but not by birth. For us first-generation folk, those who came here fleeing hardship, there is always the struggle to make a home, a real home, in what remains another's land."

"Oh, that's not true, surely," murmured Irie helplessly.

"It's very much the truth, I'm afraid. The worst of it is, you see, this time spent in the belly of the beast. Two years become four, four becomes eight, then twelve. For so many of us, it is far too late to go back. Better to give up the very idea of belonging. I truly tried to give my children roots and culture and language and traditions, but all I have succeeded in giving them is the sickness of the immigrant, the curse of the stuck-in-between. But at the same time, I can't forget what I lost. Balance, my friend. Balance."

Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt1: That year, at Christmas, my father gave me three crisp hundred-dollar bills instead of a gift. He invited me to join him and Chitra and Rupa and Piu at Disney World, where they were planning to spend part of the girls' winter vacation. I told him I couldn't go because school started up again the day after New Year's, but I didn't tell him that I checked the calendar first and realized that we would be back in plenty of time. To make up for it, I bought my half sisters ridiculously expensive presents—a record player for Rupa and a camera for Piu. Rupa cried when I told her I wasn't going to Disney World, which was where the record player and camera would be put to use. Piu put her arms around me. "I don't understand you, Didi," she said, still in her small, high voice. "What did we do wrong that makes you not want to go?" The truth was that in my eyes they had done nothing wrong, whereas I was punished by their mere existence. But I was still convinced that it was up to me to honor my mother's memory, just as they instinctively honored the man who was their father but not really mine. Still, I sensed that Chitra was relieved by my decision, and, by extension, so was my father.
written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt2: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”
written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Reason: I prefer Excerpt 2. Excerpt 1 is more direct, like a report. It's chronological, logical and easy to follow, but not as interesting - "I told them I couldn't go because school started up again." Excerpt 2 uses more sophiscated language "same laconic way." Excerpt 2 shows us how the characters are feeling, rather than telling us "eyes remained elsewhere."

written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: I held the cash, folded in my hand, and my father asked the question again. Would I like to use the gift to join them for a trip to Disney World? written_by_Devanshi.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.
written_by_Devanshi.Reason: Excerpt 2 has better writing quality than Excerpt 1. As I read Excerpt 2, I could actually visualize what was happening in the text . As I read Excerpt 1, I had to reread some parts to get a better understanding of what was being written. Excerpt 2 even included descriptive words.
